# Adapter Entry Point Review Notes

The earlier notes still start with `src/etcd/src/V3/EtcdClient.php`. It is in etcd's V3 directory and was a file we repeatedly opened while investigating the Hyperf adapter entry point. The first draft linked the directory location with the client import and took this to be the entry point for all requests; after review, we kept this line of investigation but stopped presenting it as a settled conclusion.

The dependencies visible at the top of the file are:

```php
use GuzzleHttp\Client as HttpClient;
```

`GuzzleHttp\Client` is aliased as `HttpClient`. This at least establishes the local name to search for when reading further. The problem with the first draft wasn't that it recorded the alias, but that it mistook "this name is available for use in the file" for "all requests are created here." Until we see the actual statements that use it, these two things cannot be treated as the same conclusion.

This review splits the reading within the file into two passes. The first follows only `HttpClient`: whether it appears in a property, parameter, local variable, or call expression points to a different place to look next. Properties and parameters mean the client may be supplied from outside; only a local variable warrants checking further to see whether it is created in this file. The second pass follows the post-request handling: record, in code order, whether returned content is passed straight back, transformed, or caught nearby; don't fill in the gaps based on the filename.

The sketch from that investigation is still useful, but it only shows the adjacency relationships identified so far:

```text
src/etcd/src/V3/EtcdClient.php
            |
            +-- use GuzzleHttp\Client as HttpClient
```

The arrows in the diagram are not a call graph. They do not indicate that `HttpClient` has issued requests within the file, nor that exceptions necessarily propagate out of that file. Readers following the diagram later can easily mistake an import for an execution trace, so this distinction is added here.

To assess the entry point, first read the top of the file, then locate `HttpClient` in the same file, and only then trace outward. If the client is brought in through a constructor parameter or another statement, shift attention to where it is passed in; if it is created locally, also record the configuration objects before and after the creation statement. This avoids repeatedly searching the V3 directory while missing the place that actually controls where the client comes from.

No concrete objects have yet been extracted from this file for the failure and event sections. DOC-11 contains partial notes on event exit points; when post-request behavior needs to be read alongside event handling, you can pick up there, but do not use DOC-11 in place of assessing the calls inside EtcdClient.php.

The first draft's statement that "the adapter entry point is at the import" is retained as an old lead. A safer reading now is: EtcdClient.php provides a V3 file as a starting point for further inspection, and `HttpClient` is a known direct dependency of that entry point; request construction, result handling, and failure exit points still need to be determined from the specific usage sites.

# Notes on Tracing Back to the Adapter Entry Point

This record initially focused on just one conspicuous file header: `src/etcd/src/V3/EtcdClient.php` imports the HTTP client. It has since continued to be used as a clue for tracing back to the Hyperf adapter entry point, so the initial draft's assessment has not been deleted, even though that sentence is no longer suitable as a direct conclusion about the migration.

The entry file is in etcd's V3 directory. Opening it by directory and filename initially provides only a very narrow point of reference: this concerns the V3 Etcd client, and the file header retains a dependency on a HTTP client. It does not automatically tell us when the client is created, where requests go, or how the caller obtains the result. The early record compressed these layers into a single sentence, and the later additions have mainly been unpacking that sentence.

The original snippet from the file header is as follows:

```php
use GuzzleHttp\Client as HttpClient;
```

This line can serve as the starting point for a search within the file. `GuzzleHttp\Client` appears here under the name `HttpClient`; after reading the alias, continue looking in the same file for where that name actually occurs. Property declarations, constructor parameters, local variables, and method calls may all appear to contain `HttpClient`, but they represent different adjacency relationships: properties or parameters usually lead the reader to where the object enters the file, while only local creation leads the reader to the vicinity of the local configuration. Without distinguishing these types of occurrences, tracing back through the directory will quickly turn into guesswork.

The old assessment retained from the initial draft is: since `HttpClient` appears in EtcdClient.php, this file is where requests originate. That assessment made it easier to locate the relevant code at the time, and also led people to jump straight to looking for request parameters. A later review revised it: an import only proves that the name can be used in this file, and cannot stand in for a specific call. The old assessment has not been deleted because some people still use it as their starting point to find this file; they should simply stop using it to infer the complete call chain.

The only relationship that can currently be diagrammed is:

```text
src/etcd/src/V3/EtcdClient.php
            |
            +-- use GuzzleHttp\Client as HttpClient
```

This is a file-header relationship diagram, not a runtime path diagram. The arrow points to a direct import, not a HTTP request, nor to object creation in the Hyperf container. Previously, someone read the diagram as saying "the client has already sent a request here", causing two instances of confusion over reading order: first looking outside the directory for response handling, then going back to confirm whether `HttpClient` was used within the file. The order should now be reversed, first noting the occurrences within the file by type, then deciding whether to move across files.

When tracing back, you can stay close to this file by following the order below.

- First confirm whether `HttpClient` only appears as a name in EtcdClient.php, or is already used in a property, parameter, assignment, or call. Record the specific kind you see, rather than replacing it with a single blanket term.
- If it enters the object through a parameter or property, the next stop is the statement that passes it in; at this point the file header is only a dependency hint, and you cannot leave responsibility for creation with the V3 directory.
- If you see local creation, then look at the configuration source adjacent to the creation statement. Do not assume configuration fields based on common Guzzle patterns, and do not fill in parameters that were not copied down.
- Only near the request call should you start recording where the return value goes, whether exceptions are caught, and whether an object appears that the event side can receive.

This sequence grew out of earlier misreadings, and is not a general-purpose HTTP troubleshooting procedure. The distinctive feature here is that the filename, the V3 directory, and the `HttpClient` alias appear together, making it easy to interpret "adapter entry point" as an already closed boundary. In actual reading, the entry point involves at least two questions: where the client comes from before reaching this file, and which statements this file uses it in. The earlier record did not confirm both of these together.

The second update added the approach of "look at this file first, then decide whether to trace outward". It corrected the initial draft, but still left an inaccurate impression: as though finding the uses of `HttpClient` alone would make the adapter boundary clear. The latest feedback from the field tempered that impression as well. Usage sites can tell us which direction to continue in, but result handling and failure exits still have to be read from adjacent statements, and cannot be replaced by an import, directory name, or filename.

Failure exits are a section this page has long left incomplete. No invented exception path is recorded here, nor is the ordinary behavior of the HTTP client treated as the behavior of EtcdClient.php. When you reach the actual request point, write down the nearest return handling and catch location; if the file has no corresponding snippet, the record can stop at the call boundary. The old page once described "the client dependency has been located" as "the failure path can now be traced", and that part later ceased to apply.

The event side should also be considered separately. DOC-11 is another local record adjacent to the event exit, best opened after confirming that post-request behavior needs to connect to event handling. It cannot prove in reverse that a particular event object exists in EtcdClient.php, nor can it fill in the HTTP call for this record. The relationship between the two pages is navigational: one starts from the adapter file and dependency names, while the other preserves field clues about the event exit.

For those still using this old explanation, the three easiest mistakes to make are not code errors but errors in reading order. First, treating `use` as instance creation; second, treating the V3 directory as the entire call boundary; third, deciding where exceptions or events go before finding the statements near the request. The first two mistakes both appeared in the early notes, while the third arose when readers filled in the gaps left by the old record themselves.

One working assumption from that time is retained here: EtcdClient.php is very likely a suitable entry point for continuing to trace Hyperf adapter behavior. It remains a suitable starting point because the path, the file in question, and the direct dependency are all clearly identified; but it is not synonymous with "all requests are created here". If later reading reveals that `HttpClient` is passed in from outside, immediately narrow the entry point's scope back to the relationships actually observed, then trace where it is passed in; if it turns out to be created locally, separately note the configuration objects before and after that local creation.

This page therefore retains the form of the old entry-point explanation, and has not been rewritten as the current component-boundary specification. The file-header import is a stable navigation aid, the initial draft's strong conclusion is a historical assessment that has been retained, and unrecorded calls, returns, failures, and event objects must still be established from the actual statements.

versions.body:
# Collection Ownership and Codec Conversion Decision

In discussions of component split, collection ownership and codec conversion were brought up together, but they should not be settled by the same judgment.

The starting point is paginator. The existing investigation leads to `src/paginator/src/Paginator.php`; the file appears to import `Countable`, `Hyperf\\Contract\\Arrayable`, `Hyperf\\Contract\\Jsonable`, and `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection`. This shows that the pagination object touches counts, array representations, JSON representations, and collection objects at the same time, but it still isn't enough to establish which component owns the collection implementation.

The initial working assumption was that, since the pagination object directly touches Collection, collection migration could start on the paginator side, with codec conversion handled together with the JSON representation. This assumption makes the split easier, but conflates "visible dependencies" with "ownership."

Decide as follows:

- Do not treat Paginator.php as the sole place to assign collection ownership; it is merely the adjacent entry point currently available for rechecking.
- Record collection ownership and codec conversion separately. For the former, first determine which collection implementation the post-migration consumers need; for the latter, record only whether representation conversion still passes through the existing call.
- Do not interpret the presence of `Arrayable` or `Jsonable` in this round as establishing a new codec responsibility boundary.

Keep one point open for investigation: is `Collection` stored or created by paginator, or passed in by the caller and only used by the pagination object? Without that answer, we cannot make a call on the package boundary based on the imports at the top of the file.

Keep the statement in the old notes that "paginator directly owns collection" for now; revise it during a later review.

# Decision on Collection Ownership and Encoding/Decoding

This record originally used paginator as the starting point for the collection split. After review, that starting point can stay, but the conclusion needs to be narrowed: the types listed at the top of the file only show that the object needs to work with those types. They do not, on their own, establish ownership of the collection implementation or the conversion path represented by JSON.

## Earlier assessment retained here

The draft from 2023 made an assumption to help move the split forward at the time: since `src/paginator/src/Paginator.php` imports `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection`, treat the paginator side as a candidate for collection ownership; since it also imports `Hyperf\\Contract\\Jsonable` and `Hyperf\\Contract\\Arrayable`, treat codec conversion as part of the same migration work.

This framing had two advantages. First, it left a stable file entry point for investigation; second, it did not require migrating every consumer before discussing the pagination object. But it also collapsed four different kinds of adjacency into a single package-ownership judgment: a counting interface, an array representation, a JSON representation, and a collection type are not equivalent.

The provisional decision at the time did not require moving the implementation. It only required subsequent discussions not to turn "an import exists" into "the implementation is owned here." That decision still stands. The old draft's statement that "starting with paginator is enough to determine collection ownership" is no longer used as a conclusion, but is being kept so the counterexamples later on do not appear to come out of nowhere.

## Revised position after review

The review covered only visible adjacency relationships; it did not extrapolate a complete call graph from the file location. `Countable` indicates a need for counting; `Arrayable` and `Jsonable` indicate two externally exposed representations; `Collection` indicates a collection object. They can all appear in one pagination object without requiring the same component to handle creation, conversion, and migration.

What was originally handled together has therefore been split into two questions.

| Discussion item | Draft position | Treatment after review |
| --- | --- | --- |
| collection ownership | paginator can be used to determine ownership | Retain paginator only as a starting point for rechecking; assess ownership by looking at which implementation consumers adopt after migration |
| codec conversion | Move it along with the JSON representation | First identify the interfaces used in representation conversion, then decide whether component-level changes are needed |
| `Arrayable` / `Jsonable` | Directly establish responsibility for conversion | Only show that the object needs the corresponding representations; do not establish the division of responsibility on their own |
| `Collection` | Directly defines the new collection boundary | An object that needs further tracing, not a conclusion about the boundary |

"Starting point for rechecking" has a narrow meaning here: when opening `Paginator.php`, first confirm whether these direct dependencies still exist, then follow the current references to determine how the object obtains its collection. It does not make paginator responsible for every collection issue.

## Options previously kept open

Option A was to give paginator provisional ownership of collection and migrate codec conversion along with the pagination object. It would keep the scope of the split small, but could easily misrepresent consumers' choice of collection implementation as an internal decision by the pagination component.

Option B was to record only paginator's type adjacency, determine collection ownership from what consumers adopt after migration, and put codec conversion through a separate interface review. It does not provide a directory that can be moved immediately, but avoids tying output representation to data ownership.

This round adopts Option B. Not because paginator is unrelated to collections, but because the available material does not establish that it owns the collection implementation. This page does not decide how to implement codec conversion either; the interface discussion adjacent to payload packers is left to DOC-14. This page only records why that cannot be inferred from paginator's import list.

## Additional review notes

One challenge raised during review is worth keeping on record: if the same object can be converted both to an array and to JSON, does that mean it is responsible for all encoding itself? The answer is no. Representation interfaces describe the shapes an object can provide; they do not automatically identify which component handles the underlying conversion. This challenge overturns the draft's reasoning, not paginator's dependency on representation interfaces.

Another challenge was whether paginator's imports must change whenever a caller uses a different collection implementation after migration. This was not confirmed in this round. That does not justify stating in advance that they "will definitely be replaced" or "will never be replaced."

## Provisional boundaries

We are retaining three actionable boundaries:

1. Gather evidence for collection ownership discussions from the collection implementations consumers adopt; do not infer ownership directly from a single import.
2. paginator is a starting point for rechecking type adjacency. It can help uncover issues, but is not a substitute for determining ownership.
3. Record codec conversion as a separate issue. Unless a specific conversion interface or call chain can be identified, do not present references to `Jsonable` and `Arrayable` as a migration decision.

The old paragraphs still explain why paginator was prioritized at the time; they should no longer be cited as a conclusion about component boundaries.

versions.body:
# Decision on Collection Ownership and Encoding/Decoding

The fact that paginator was once used in troubleshooting is not the only reason this decision record has been retained. Midway through the component split, collection ownership and codec conversion were often mentioned in the same breath: wherever the collection moved, conversion of JSON would move with it. This was convenient shorthand in discussions, but it left later readers unable to tell which parts were working assumptions at the time, which had been reviewed, and which had remained unresolved throughout.

The old paragraphs are retained here mainly to keep statements such as "paginator directly owns the collection" visible. That statement helped narrow the scope of investigation, but it also mistook adjacency between types for a boundary of responsibility. People still reach this page through old links, and deleting it would leave later corrections with nothing to refer back to.

## Initial Focus: The Collection Next to the Pagination Object

The earliest notes began with `src/paginator/src/Paginator.php`. At that point, there was no attempt to draw a complete dependency graph, only to list the objects visible at the top of the file: `Countable`, `Hyperf\\Contract\\Arrayable`, `Hyperf\\Contract\\Jsonable`, and `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection`. The pagination object dealt with counts, array representations, JSON representations, and collection objects at the same time, making it easy to see it as a place that "wraps both the collection and encoding."

At the time, the practical pressure in the component split was to first find an accessible entry point. paginator met that requirement: issue titles pointed to it, and `Collection` also appeared among the adjacent dependencies. So the draft first set out a working assessment: collection ownership could be determined starting with paginator, and codec conversion could be handled alongside the JSON representation.

The value of this assessment lay only in setting the order of investigation. It did not establish where `Collection` was created, did not establish whether the pagination object managed its lifecycle, and did not establish whether conversion of the JSON representation was performed by the pagination object. The draft did not spell out each of these gaps, so on later readings it sounded like a settled decision about package boundaries.

The initial decision was conservative: do not move the implementation, and do not declare ownership based on file paths; for now, keep paginator as the entry point for investigating collection issues. At the time, "investigation entry point" and "owner" were not given distinct labels, which led to later misreadings.

## The Retained Old Proposal: Tying the Two Things Together

The passage below reflects the original intent of the old proposal, is preserved in its original location, and will not be rewritten to match the current position:

> paginator already interacts with Collection, so the collection migration can be consolidated here; the object also implements array and JSON representations, so codec conversion should also be assigned to this component, and callers only need to switch to the new entry point.

At the time, this passage offered a very direct path forward. If paginator was where collections and representations converged, the split could be treated as a single-point change. It also implied an unstated premise: whenever an object exposes a JSON representation, representation conversion belongs to the component containing that object.

This premise was later overturned. Saying that an object can provide a JSON representation and saying that the object is responsible for all encoding steps are two different claims. `Jsonable` can only show that interface adjacency exists in the form of JSON; it cannot, on its own, show that conversion occurs inside paginator, nor can it determine which component should take responsibility for conversion. Similarly, `Arrayable` indicates that an array form can be obtained, and is not automatically tied to ownership of the collection implementation.

The old plan was not removed from the document, because it explains why the early discussions always listed collection ownership and codec conversion side by side. The migration order should no longer be inferred from this passage. It is a working plan that is no longer valid, not a set of operational instructions.

## Two questions left by the early review

When the old plan was first brought up for discussion, the questions did not focus on "whether people liked the new directories", but on whether the reasoning went beyond the existing material.

The first question was: if a pagination object imports `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection`, what exactly does that tell us? At a minimum, it shows that the object needs to work with a collection type. But "work with" could mean storing, receiving, returning, or only using it in local computations; looking at the import alone cannot distinguish among these possibilities. Describing it directly as ownership replaces several possibilities with an unsupported conclusion.

The second question was: are `Arrayable` and `Jsonable` sufficient to assign codec conversion to paginator? The answer at the time was "interpret it this way for now, pending a review of the callers". This answer should be treated as a deferral, not confirmation. It acknowledged the need to examine the callers further, yet used a tone suggesting that the decision was already settled in the same paragraph, leading some people later to treat the deferral as a conclusion.

A brief note after the review once read "put both the collection and codec on the paginator side, and adjust later if counterexamples emerge". This was also part of the old position. It was not implemented as an explicit component migration decision; it merely deferred the risk until later. This note is retained to explain why the first thing sought during the reassessment was not new directories, but counterexamples.

## Reassessment in 2024: type adjacency does not equal ownership

The follow-up review returned to the same file, but changed how the question was framed. Instead of asking "is this a collection component", it examined the direct dependencies separately:

- `Countable` corresponds to the requirement to be countable. It is adjacent to the collection object, but cannot select an implementation for the collection.
- `Hyperf\\Contract\\Arrayable` corresponds to the array form. It provides clues about representation capabilities, not an explanation of the collection lifecycle.
- `Hyperf\\Contract\\Jsonable` corresponds to the JSON form. It allows an object to expose a JSON representation, but does not automatically place all codec conversion in the current file.
- `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection` is the object term closest to collection ownership, but "being referenced" is still different from "being owned here".

The review did not find a new, complete call chain; instead, it ruled out the overly strong inferences in the earlier draft. The available material is sufficient to say that paginator is directly adjacent to these four types of objects; it is not sufficient to determine creation relationships, sole ownership after migration, or the specific location of the encoding steps. This distinction is narrow, but it is why this page continued to be cited afterward.

The review also retained a potentially confusing statement: "paginator is the entry point for collection". If this means an entry point for investigation, the statement can still be used; if it means the implementation owner, it is inaccurate. Subsequent records consistently called the former an entry point for tracing back, and no longer used it as a substitute for component ownership.

This does not relegate `Paginator.php` to being an irrelevant file. On the contrary, it remains the most convenient way to navigate adjacent relationships: when starting from object terms such as `Collection`, `Arrayable`, and `Jsonable`, you can first confirm whether the file still retains the same dependency structure in the frozen revision. This step alone, however, cannot settle the ownership question.

## The two approaches compared at the time

| Approach | Benefits available at the time | Problems that emerged later |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treat paginator as the owner of both collections and conversion | Made the scope of the split appear concentrated, making the first batch of changes easy to plan | Conflated type references, object representation, and implementation ownership, obscuring which collection implementation callers adopted |
| Use paginator only as an entry point to adjacent dependencies, and confirm ownership and conversion separately | Avoided turning an import into a conclusion about a component | Required separately tracing what consumers adopted and the representation interfaces, with no short-term answer for "migrating everything in one go" |

This page chose the second approach after the review. The decision was not "paginator is no longer involved in collection issues", but "do not declare collection ownership based on paginator's import list". These two statements seem similar, but their effects on the split differ: the former allows object relationships to continue to be traced through the file, while the latter refuses to let file location stand in for object relationships.

codec conversion is also retained under the second approach. It appears alongside collection ownership because the pagination object has adjacency to both the collection and representation interfaces; this does not make them the same responsibility unit. Conversion issues should first be traced to the interface or call actually traversed, and only then should component movement be discussed. Without that object relationship, this page does not make the decision on its behalf.

## An Incomplete Verification Record

Earlier records proposed using existing tests or examples to exercise collection ownership, then filling in the user paths that were not covered. This suggestion did not produce a complete result that could be written into this page; therefore, it cannot be rewritten as "tests have already proven paginator ownership." Its only purpose was to clarify the verification target: distinguish which collection implementation the migrated consumers selected from what types paginator can currently see.

codec conversion has the same unfinished aspect. Existing calls are described as still retaining a conversion requirement, but there is no material placing any specific conversion step at `Paginator.php`. Therefore, the early plan to "migrate together with JSON" remained at the proposal level and was not elevated to an implementation decision on this page.

This record was once misread as a failed incident. More accurately, it was a review that did not gather all the object relationships. There was no anomaly to attribute; only one overly strong conclusion was withdrawn, and two issues were separated and retained for continued follow-up.

## Meeting Margin Notes and Correction Trail

The most useful margin note from the meeting was: "Start with a working hypothesis, then look for counterexamples." It is included here not to turn the discussion into meeting minutes, but because it genuinely changed how this page was written. The old proposal treated paginator as the shared ownership point; the counterexample is not another better-sounding component name, but that the semantics carried by the four dependency types are not the same.

Another margin note was: "What an interface can return is not the same as which layer completes the conversion." This statement was used to correct the misreading of `Jsonable`. It does not specify the final destination of codec conversion, so it should not be excerpted as a new migration rule.

The review feedback added later required writing "the collection implementation adopted by callers" and "the collection dependency visible to paginator" separately. This correction did not rewrite the old chapter, but instead appended a verification section after the old proposal. Preserving this not-quite-consistent texture between the earlier and later sections is more useful than smoothing the document into a uniform specification: readers can understand why the old link led them to paginator, and can also see why that location cannot make the final determination.

## Decisions Still in Effect

As of this pass, the decisions retained on this page are as follows.

First, the evidence for collection ownership should be completed by determining which collection implementation the migrated paginator consumers adopt. `Paginator.php` can serve as an entry point for identifying collection adjacency, but cannot alone serve as proof of implementation ownership.

Second, handle codec conversion separately. Array representation, JSON representation, collection objects, and counting capability can all appear in the same paginator object; their co-occurrence is not enough to show that they must be migrated in the same batch, much less that they are owned by the same component.

Third, the old plan is not to be used as the basis for execution. When explaining the history, you may cite why it tied the two things together; when making a new component determination, you must return to object relationships and consumer adoption rather than repeat the old plan's shortcut conclusion.

Fourth, discussion of the interface layer related to payload packers is not covered on this page. DOC-14 can serve as adjacent review entry points, but this page does not work backward from them to fill in conversion details that do not exist inside the paginator.

These decisions deliberately do not provide a blanket answer that "all collections should be moved somewhere." The existing material supports only separating reasoning that should not be combined. For an old decision page that has been cited for a long time, this is more reliable than fabricating a complete migration map.

## Current requirements added in the year 2025

The earlier records preserve the old assumptions, review questions, and one incomplete verification. They explain the history; they do not change the current requirements for post-migration users. The following fact must currently be kept in the implementation and review of component split:

Hyperf\Collection\Collection is the collection implementation used by migrated paginator and framework consumers.

This requirement is placed later in the document because it was not a conclusion reached in the early draft. Nor does it mean that "`Paginator.php` owns the collection implementation": the former identifies the collection implementation used by the migrated paginator and framework consumers, while the latter remains a responsibility question that must be determined through object relationships.

This correction also limits the scope in which the old plan can be used. The old plan can help explain why the investigation started with paginator, but it can no longer be used to claim that `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection` should remain the post-migration implementation choice. The import retained in the frozen path is a local navigation aid from the old revision and should not override what post-migration consumers adopted.

Codec conversion was not automatically assigned an owner along with this requirement. The current material provides no specific alternative conversion entry point, so here we simply maintain the separation decision already made: the conclusion about adoption of the collection implementation is clear; responsibility for representation conversion still needs to be checked against the actual interface relationships.

The current evolution can be condensed into the following state relationship. It represents only the handling changes recorded on this page; it does not depict adjacent issues as migrations that have been completed:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> paginator
    paginator --> old_plan
    old_plan --> review
    review --> split
    split --> current
    split --> unresolved
    state paginator as "Paginator.php Direct dependency entry point"
    state old_plan as "Collection and conversion tied together"
    state review as "Type adjacency review"
    state split as "Record ownership and conversion separately"
    state current as "Post-migration collection requirements"
    state unresolved as "Representation conversion entry point awaiting verification"
```

## Adjacent issue, not yet split out

There is another adjacent issue that has not been settled on this page: when paginator exposes both array and JSON forms, do consumers see the representation of the collection itself, or the representation organized by the pagination object? This affects the direction of the investigation into codec conversion, but the existing material does not provide enough information to choose between the two.

This question should no longer be recast as "JSON must be performed in paginator" or "JSON must be performed by the collection". It only shows that object representation and implementation responsibility still need to be distinguished. If a subsequent interface review fills in the object relationships, the decision should be made in the corresponding interface record, rather than going back and revising the initial assessment on this old page.

## Appendix of old examples: retained for readers following old links

**Old example one: using import to determine ownership.**

Earlier investigations often narrowed the scope by reasoning that "the file imports `Hyperf\\Utils\\Collection`, so the collection belongs to the component containing that file". This approach is still useful for finding the entry point: it can lead readers to the types adjacent to paginator. But it mistakes "referencing a type" for "owning that type's implementation". This example no longer applies to ownership decisions, and is retained only because old issue names and call names may still bring people here.

**Old example two: using the JSON interface to determine where conversion occurs.**

Another earlier claim was "if an object implements `Hyperf\\Contract\\Jsonable`, codec conversion is the responsibility of the component containing that object". This claim once made it seem that collection ownership and codec conversion could be handled together. Upon later review, it was found to prove at most that the object provides a JSON representation, not the location of the conversion step or the boundaries of responsibility. This example has been retired; it does not deny the existence of a JSON representation, it only denies that component ownership can be inferred directly from that interface's name.

**Old example three: Treating array form as a stand-in for a collection implementation.**

Earlier notes placed `Hyperf\\Contract\\Arrayable` and `Collection` in the same column, as though together they described "collection output". This overlooks the possibility that the pagination object itself may also construct an array form. This classification is no longer used. Now during verification, the array representation, the JSON representation, counting and the collection implementation are recorded separately, before determining which relationships are actually connected within a given component.

The examples in the appendix do not have to be followed. They are parts of this page that remain useful, but are already outdated: they can help identify where the old conclusions came from, but cannot replace judgments about the current implementation.

Finally we still use the original local entry point: when revisiting earlier judgments, start with the direct dependencies of `src/paginator/src/Paginator.php`; when assessing collection adoption after the migration, look at the actual objects used by paginator and framework consumers; when assessing codec conversion, separately examine the relationships traversed by the representation interfaces. These three matters can inform one another, but must no longer be written up as a single conclusion.

# Application Container Serialization Troubleshooting Tree

After the component split, when the container received by callers differs from what was expected at startup, first preserve the evidence under application container ownership. If serializer hooks come up in the same round, note them separately first; don't connect the two as a single cause.

The old entry point starts at `src/utils/src/ApplicationContext.php`. The file header shows:

```php
use Psr\Container\ContainerInterface;
use TypeError;
```

First find where callers read the container. When the setting action can be found, record the setting and reading sides side by side; if only the reading side is found, you can say only that the current read succeeded, not that it is still the original object.

```text
container symptom
├─ Found the setting and reading locations
│  └─ Record the objects at both ends; prepare to compare
├─ Found only the reading location
│  └─ Record that the read succeeded; ownership unconfirmed
└─ Cannot find the reading location
   └─ Continue from references to ApplicationContext
```

In the earlier notes, "object can be retrieved" was recorded as usable. That only rules out the case where the object cannot be retrieved at all. Don't write "usable" as if the object's identity had been verified.

Put serializer hooks on a separate line: they require an input that directly triggers them and the actual output. Without this pair of pieces of evidence, don't use the hooks description to fill in the container assessment.

# Application container serialization troubleshooting tree

The old version put application container ownership and serializer hooks on the same troubleshooting sheet. After review, the entry points remain, but "appeared in the same round" is no longer treated as evidence of a connection. Whether the container is still the object that was set, and whether the hooks produce different results, are two questions that require different evidence.

## Entry points carried over from 2023

The search originally started at `src/utils/src/ApplicationContext.php`. The visible direct dependency was:

```php
use Psr\Container\ContainerInterface;
use TypeError;
```

The step at the time was simple: search for `ContainerInterface` and see whether the caller could retrieve a container. This is still a valid starting point because it brings the investigation back to the read operation; it does not answer where the container was set.

The old tree is retained below. It came from a case that mixed together "can't retrieve anything" and "can retrieve it, but something seems off":

```text
Container issue observed
├─ ApplicationContext can retrieve an object
│  └─ Initially mark as usable
└─ Cannot retrieve an object
   └─ Return to the Context entry point
```

"Usable" is no longer enough to support further conclusions here. A successful read only shows that an object was retrieved at this point. It does not show which set operation the object came from, or whether it is the same instance as the one that was set.

## Notes added in the margin

Later, someone added two lines beside the old tree:

```text
Read succeeded: retain the read-side object
Set side not found: ownership unconfirmed
```

These two lines are more useful than "Context is working." The first records the read that occurred; the second defines a stopping point. If the set side cannot be found, do not use `TypeError`, coroutine behavior, or output from the hooks as a substitute for comparing the objects.

In the past, `TypeError` was treated as supporting evidence of an identity change. That interpretation is no longer used. A type error can show that a particular interaction did not meet expectations; it cannot tell us whether the set side and the read side have the same object. The absence of a type error does not prove that ownership is correct either.

## An incomplete follow-up investigation

This round included an attempt to confirm ownership using only the caller's result. A usable container was available on the read side, but no set-side object had been retained. The attempt was inconclusive.

It ruled out only "there is no object here at all." It did not rule out the object changing at an earlier point, nor did it prove that the retrieved object still matched what had been set. The statement "application container confirmed" in the old draft should be treated as obsolete:

> **Obsolete:** A successful read is enough to confirm application container ownership.

This sentence is retained for anyone arriving through an old link, to show where the mistake occurred. The next step is not to add an overall status to Context, but to find the set operation, retain the set-side object, and compare it with the read-side object.

## Hooks do not fill gaps in container evidence

A margin note from the same period read: **Retain the container first, then ask about the hook.** The intent was to avoid losing the existing container evidence when the evidence for the hooks was incomplete. It did not mean the hooks were unimportant, or that the hooks necessarily came after the container operations.

The serializer hooks branch collects only two things: the input that directly triggered them, and the tool's actual output. If either is missing, stop at the hooks branch. The container branch collects the set-side and read-side objects. These two types of evidence cannot substitute for each other.

| Observation | What to retain first at this stage | Conclusions not yet supported |
|---|---|---|
| application container ownership | Set-side object, read-side object | Why the objects differ, or whether a replacement has already occurred |
| serializer hooks | Direct input, actual output | Whether the container caused that result |
| coroutine lifecycle | A trace already linked to this call | That it necessarily explains either of the first two items |

For the table above, "all evidence present" does not mean the objects are the same. Comparison can begin only when the objects from both ends are available; the hooks' input and output must be retained as a pair before that result can be reviewed. When both lines of investigation appear in the same case record, the order of discovery can be retained, but one "reproduced" claim cannot cover both.

# Application Container Serialization Troubleshooting Tree

In early component split investigations, application container ownership and serializer hooks were often written on the same line. Both were discovered near the old Context entry point, so the initial troubleshooting notes grouped them together. The habit of starting at that entry point was retained; the practice of directly treating the two observations as cause and effect was not.

`src/utils/src/ApplicationContext.php` remains the starting point for tracing back. The file header shows:

```php
use Psr\Container\ContainerInterface;
use TypeError;
```

After seeing `ContainerInterface`, first distinguish whether the investigation is looking for the container that was set, the container that was read, or is merely recording a single result from serializer hooks. `TypeError` can be included in an anomaly record, but is not a criterion for container identity. Save container object relationships and hooks inputs and outputs separately; leave the question of whether a single call connects them until actual references or a trace appear.

## Original Notes for 2023-06

The first version addressed only a very narrow question: the caller could obtain an object, but someone thought it did not look like the one expected at startup. The set side was not recorded separately, nor was the read side placed alongside the set operation. The notes at the time read "Retrievable from Context, keep observing".

This was a working approach for narrowing the scope, not a rule of behavior. The old tree is preserved unchanged:

```text
A container anomaly is observed
├─ ApplicationContext can retrieve an object
│  └─ Record it as usable for now
└─ Cannot retrieve an object
   └─ Return to the Context entry point
```

This tree can distinguish "no object at all" from "an object exists but its identity is in doubt". The drawback is that once the second case falls under "usable", later readers can easily interpret usable as meaning the original object is still there. The old tree was not deleted, because historical notes often contain only the words "Retrievable from Context"; when coming back from those notes, readers need to see where the assessment stopped at the time.

In the margin of the same sheet was a line: **Save the container first, then ask about the hook.** It only specifies the order of preservation. When the inputs to hooks have not yet been saved, the container state should not be lost along with them. It is neither a declaration of priority nor a statement that hooks are unrelated to the container.

An undirected line was also drawn early on:

```text
container ?  →  serializer hooks ?
```

At the time, it only served as a reminder that the two items had appeared side by side in a single investigation. Without a set operation, a read operation, inputs, or outputs, this is not a causal arrow. It is retained to prevent later revisions from once again copying an ambiguous notation as a conclusion.

## 2023 On-Call Marginal Notes

While on call, we often start in `ApplicationContext.php` and search for `ContainerInterface` to check whether the caller can obtain a particular container. This step is still useful: it can confirm whether the read operation exists and bring the investigation back to actual references.

Two short side notes were later added to the old tree:

```text
Read succeeded: retain the read-side object
Setup side not found: ownership unconfirmed
```

These two lines replaced blanket wording such as "Context is normal". A successful read can rule out one local issue: the object is not completely inaccessible at the current location. It cannot stand in for the setup site, nor can it answer whether the object has been replaced, when it changed, or whether it is related to a particular coroutine symptom.

On one occasion, the read side obtained a usable object, but there was no setup-side evidence at all. This counterexample did not show that the object was necessarily different; it showed that the old procedure had skipped over the missing side. Afterward, "has a return value" was followed by "does not mean identity has been checked". Kept in the on-call log, this sentence is more likely than a long explanation to trigger the next action: look for the setup side.

Another side note was "hooks do not block container checks". This also has limits. Evidence about the container can be saved first, which does not mean hooks are being ignored; if hooks already have direct inputs and actual outputs, their own line of investigation can continue. If all there is for hooks is the statement "the results differ", stop at the hooks branch, and do not use it to explain the read-side object.

## Where tracing back through 2024-04 failed

During the second revision, an attempt was made to infer ownership from the caller's results. The approach was to record the container obtained by the read side, then use that to determine whether the setup operation was stable. This attempt did not produce a usable conclusion.

The failure was not in the exception text or in the tools. The evidence covered only the read side. A successful read can show that the current call obtained an object; it cannot answer which setup operation the object came from, nor whether it is still the instance from that setup.

The old draft once contained the sentence "the application container has been confirmed". It is explicitly marked as deprecated here:

> **Deprecated:** A successful read is enough to confirm application container ownership.

The original sentence is retained so that anyone arriving through a historical entry point can see what is being corrected. When the setup operation cannot be found, do not add a blanket status to Context, only record that ownership is unconfirmed and stop there.

There was also a quick-screening proposal in the same round that was not adopted: in the absence of `TypeError`, temporarily treat the container as normal. This proposal was not included in the operating procedure. The file references `TypeError`, but that does not mean a type error can describe object identity relationships. Even without a type error, the setup side may still be missing; even when a type error occurs, it does not follow that the object has necessarily been replaced.

The tree left from that time was later used for a while:

```text
A container-related symptom appears on the read side
├─ Object present
│  ├─ Setup-side evidence available
│  │  └─ Compare the objects on both sides
│  └─ No setup-side evidence
│     └─ Provisionally record "read succeeded, ownership unconfirmed"
└─ No object
   └─ Return to the actual reference to ApplicationContext
```

The container section of this tree is still usable. It does not list serializer hooks separately, and someone later appended hooks observations after the "Object present" branch, leading readers to mistakenly believe that the two shared a stopping condition. It is no longer written this way.

## Withdrawn combined format

There was a proposal to group container, coroutine lifecycle and serializer hooks together under "Context anomalies", with all three documented in the same record. The proposal was not pursued.

It was withdrawn not because the three never overlap, but because the forms of evidence that need to be retained differ. container needs the object relationships on both the setup and read sides; serializer hooks need the direct inputs and the actual tool outputs; coroutine lifecycle is only worth including in the same round of investigation when an existing trace connects to the current call. When all three were crammed into one field, someone later seeing "reproduced" could not tell which phenomenon had actually been reproduced.

The old scheme is still shown here:

```text
Context anomalies
├─ container
├─ coroutine
└─ serializer hooks
```

This classification is no longer used operationally. When coroutine state appears at runtime, it is not assumed to explain container identity; serializer hooks are no longer called a "Context branch" either. If the trace does not connect to the current setup or read operation, coroutine lifecycle remains only a related issue.

## Counterexamples documented after the review

A subsequent review required separating "usable" from "the same". The counterexample was a usable object on the read side, with no setup-side evidence available. The old steps would classify it as "usable", but it could not prove that the original instance was still present. This counterexample did not prove that the object had changed either; it only limited what could be said at the time.

Another counterexample came from how hooks were documented. On one occasion, only "serializer hooks result differences in the current version" was recorded, without saving the input that directly triggered them. Such a description can serve as a case awaiting additional evidence, but cannot be treated as the cause of a container anomaly. Even if the two phenomena appeared in the same regression run, a hooks record without the input still cannot explain the difference between the setup side and the read side.

After the review, two short annotations were added next to the historical form:

- Append after "return value exists":**does not mean identity has been verified**;
- Append after "hooks differ":**add the missing inputs and outputs first**.

The first annotation directs the investigation toward both sides of container, and the second directs it toward the evidence for hooks. When both sets of evidence remain incomplete, each investigation stops in its own branch.

## 2025-09 Card Addendum

HCF-203 is the routine inspection entry point for application container ownership. The card continues to use `Hyperf\Context\ApplicationContext` as a search term to bring the investigation back to existing paths and previous records; it cannot replace actual confirmation on both the setting and reading sides.

The records for 2025-09 show that the application container check has already been run, but one ownership point remains unconfirmed, and the input and output remain in the coroutine lifecycle trace. Here, "check executed" only means that the check ran; it cannot be expanded to mean that ownership is complete. The trace is an adjacent clue; unless it is connected to the setting and reading actions, it cannot support a conclusion about the object relationship.

During the same month, the card's handling direction was adjusted because the issue fell in another part of the implementation. This change explains why the card changed its handling direction; it does not mean that part of the implementation has been fully located. For the current case, continue to use the setting and reading actions found this time as the basis.

## 2025-10 to 11 Hooks Stop Point

HCF-219 records the differences in results for the current versions of serializer hooks. This card requires running source code that directly triggers the hooks through the existing entry point and saving the input and the tool's actual output. This requirement cannot be reduced to "looks different": without input, the output cannot be explained; without output, the input cannot by itself show that a difference was produced.

After the interface review in 10 month, the record still lacked concrete input, so it did not proceed to implementation. In 11 month, the CI queue was stuck, and the local result was not adopted further. This stop point is narrowly scoped: local materials may be retained, but they cannot be used to advance the hooks implementation decision. It does not change the progress of the container branch, nor does it let the hooks branch close itself out based on a single local result.

If two phenomena appear at the same site at the same time, their temporal order can be retained—for example, discovering the object on the reading side first and obtaining the hooks output later; or saving the hooks input first and locating the setting action only afterward. The order helps with review, but does not automatically establish causality.

| Field | First piece of evidence | Second piece of evidence | Stop conditions |
|---|---|---|---|
| application container ownership | Object on the setter or getter side | Object at the other end | Either end is missing, or the objects cannot be compared directly |
| serializer hooks | Directly triggered input | Actual output from the tool | Input or output is missing, or the local result was not subsequently used |
| coroutine lifecycle | trace already associated with the current call | Clue connected to the setter or getter | trace appears only in an adjacent location and is not connected to the current call |

Here, "second piece of evidence" is not there just to fill out the table. The two ends of a container are the minimum evidence for an object relationship; the hook input and output are a set of results that can be reviewed afterward. Even if one branch has all its evidence, it does not fill the gap in the other branch.

## 2026-02 Field branch

The tree below replaces the old "continue as soon as it is available" tree. First enter a branch based on observable symptoms, then find the evidence missing from that branch.

```text
Scenario: questions about exception boundaries after component split
│
├─ The observed behavior concerns application container ownership
│  │
│  ├─ Has the set operation been located?
│  │  ├─ No
│  │  │  └─ Record that the setting side is missing; trace back from actual references to ApplicationContext; stop
│  │  └─ Yes
│  │     ├─ Has the read operation been located?
│  │     │  ├─ No
│  │     │  │  └─ Record that the reading side is missing; stop
│  │     │  └─ Yes
│  │     │     ├─ Can the objects at both ends be compared directly?
│  │     │     │  ├─ No
│  │     │     │  │  └─ Retain the object evidence; do not determine ownership; stop
│  │     │     │  └─ Yes
│  │     │     │     └─ Proceed based on the current object relationships
│  │
│  └─ Is a coroutine lifecycle trace also available?
│     ├─ Yes
│     │  └─ Record trace observations separately, do not use them as a substitute for object comparison
│     └─ No
│        └─ Do not add a coroutine explanation
│
└─ The observed behavior concerns serializer hooks
   │
   ├─ Is input that directly triggers it available?
   │  ├─ No
   │  │  └─ Supply the input; stop
   │  └─ Yes
   │     ├─ Is actual tool output available?
   │     │  ├─ No
   │     │  │  └─ Save the input, wait for output; stop
   │     │  └─ Yes
   │     │     ├─ Were the local results not used further?
   │     │     │  ├─ Yes
   │     │     │  │  └─ Retain the evidence, do not proceed to an implementation decision
   │     │     │  └─ No
   │     │     │     └─ Recheck the differences using the evidence from hooks themselves
```

"Stop" in the tree does not mean giving up on troubleshooting. It means that the current branch cannot support a stronger conclusion; the next step is only to supply the evidence missing from that branch. If one side is missing for the container, locate that side; if hooks are missing input or output, supply the corresponding item.

## Current guidance

Once the setting and reading actions have been located, and the objects at both ends can be compared directly, handle it as follows: Hyperf\Context\ApplicationContext owns the process-wide PSR container and returns the exact instance assigned through setContainer().

This rule only addresses application container ownership. It does not define the input format for serializer hooks, explain the coroutine lifecycle trace, or turn `TypeError` into a criterion for container identity.

Actual tracing back still starts from the relevant references to `src/utils/src/ApplicationContext.php`, followed by confirmation of the setting and reading actions. Dependencies visible in the files are sufficient to identify the entry point, but the object comparison cannot be skipped. For hooks, do not omit the direct input just because the container has already been concluded; for the container, do not omit the setting side just because the hooks already have output.

## Adjacent items not yet separated

The coroutine lifecycle trace mentioned in the old record has not yet been organized here as an independent flow. It is adjacent to the unconfirmed items HCF-203, but it is not the default cause of the container or hooks. Later, if the trace can point to a call connected to the setting or reading action, add it to the corresponding branch; without this connection, continue with the current tree, leaving them in their respective branches.

## Retained old form

The following two items are only for identifying historical records, not current operating steps.

### Appendix A: Old "Context available" marker

The old form once had a column:

```text
ApplicationContext object retrievable: yes / no
```

After "yes" was entered, the form defaulted to recording the container as available. This field can now at most help determine whether the reading action produced a result; it cannot indicate that ownership has been confirmed. When maintaining the old form, keep the setting side, reading side, and object comparison as three separate items instead of using one "available" field to cover them.

### Appendix B: Merged exception description

The old note once put the following content on one line:

```text
Context / coroutine / serializer hooks
```

This line was once used for temporary keyword searches, but later ceased to be used as a category. Container issues go back to object relationships; hooks issues go back to inputs and outputs; coroutine items are listed separately only when a trace already exists. Retain the old note so that, when entering from a historical link, the material can be split back into the correct places.

# Channel and Composer Migration Procedure

This record originally started from the old entry point. In the earlier investigation, both the issue name and the call name pointed to `src/pool/src/Channel.php`, so the migration checks initially centered on this file as well. That version treated it as the common destination after the component split, even putting lifecycle issues and failures to discover composer metadata on the same investigation track. This sequence later proved unreliable: finding the file does not mean the caller gets the same Channel; getting metadata back does not mean the coroutine state has ended as expected.

The direct adjacency recorded in the file header has not changed:

```php
use Hyperf\Contract\ConnectionInterface;
use Hyperf\Engine\Channel as CoChannel;
use Hyperf\Utils\Coroutine;
use SplQueue;
```

During migration, still start from `src/pool/src/Channel.php`, but treat it only as a checkpoint on the old path. First save the old directory references and the raw return status of composer metadata, then confirm whether the same compatible caller can discover the post-split component entry point. If discovery fails, do not recast a path error as a lifecycle error. Instead, first restore the old dependencies or directory references, retain the failure output, and then rerun a separate channel lifecycle check. The full path of the new entry point was not recorded here, so batches can only be distinguished by caller and entry point type; a package name cannot be filled in here.

The earlier investigation also assumed that "closing" only required clearing the externally held queue. A later review examined the object relationships separately: the queue, coroutine, and underlying channel are adjacent objects, and cleanup order affects the next use. The behavior record currently cited reads:

Hyperf\Coroutine\Channel\Manager caches channels by integer identifier, creates them with its configured size, and flushes them by closing each channel.

This note should come after the lifecycle check, rather than being used to draw conclusions about directory discovery for composer. `integer identifier` is the index criterion for cache lookups, and configured size is a parameter used at creation; flush closes each channel in turn. This addresses the relationship between Manager and channel and cannot replace the entry point check for compatible callers.

```text
Old path: src/pool/src/Channel.php
  ├─ channel lifecycle check
  └─ composer metadata discovery
Post-split component entry point: full path not recorded
  ├─ Discovery by compatible callers
  └─ Lifecycle review
```

The actual migration can follow the original sequence below:

1. From the old path, confirm the identifier, size, and close action used by the caller. Do not change the caller yet.
2. Perform composer metadata discovery on the post-split entry point, and save the relative path and the tool's return status.
3. Rerun the lifecycle with the same caller, recording the results for creation, use, and flush separately. Do not combine metadata failure and channel close failure into a single conclusion.
4. Only remove the old directory references once both entry point discovery and lifecycle results can be matched up; if either fails, restore the old dependencies and retain the failure output for the new entry point.

The old steps may still appear in knowledge base search results, especially the statement "all issues lead back to `Channel.php`." It explains why the investigation started here at the time, but is not a suitable basis for deciding component ownership now. The old failed call to composer metadata also only shows that the discovery entry point was still unresolved at the time. This record does not contain the new package name, a complete list of callers, or batch results from a successful migration; those gaps remain open.

After the last check, responsibilities were narrowed to just two areas: check object lifecycles on the Channel side, and split entry points and metadata on the Composer side. Remove the old path only after both sides pass. It is not a verified description of the implementation: there was no stable output at the time, and the "shared entry point" was only a proposed rollout gate.

The original idea started with `src/utils/src/Stringable.php`. The earlier investigation notes pointed to this file based on issue names and call names; the top of the file shows four direct imports: `ArrayAccess`, `Closure`, `Hyperf\Macroable\Macroable`, and `JsonSerializable`. On that basis, the initial draft treated it as an observation point for the chainable value object, then put string output and file writes in a single record. That inference made things easy at the time: if value wrapping changed after the split, calling Fang Ke could reveal the difference in the chained result first; if incomplete writes also appeared, they could directly block this rollout.

## What we planned to record

String samples did not require assuming in advance that a particular method definitely handled Unicode. Each record only needed to state the input, the chained calls it actually went through, and the value the caller ultimately saw. The first batch of inputs should include at least one set of non-ASCII characters and one set of ordinary inputs; the original values and the values after the calls should be kept side by side, rather than just recording "Unicode issue" with nothing to compare.

The old criteria on the file side were stricter, but also cruder. A write only qualified for this round of samples if both its before and after states were clear and no intermediate content was mistaken for the final result. The initial draft intended to store this right alongside the string samples: string differences and write differences appearing around the same input would first be treated as a single interface risk. This arrangement did not state that `Stringable.php` initiated file writes, nor did it define the file object's responsibilities; it was only meant to let reviewers use one set of material to decide whether to pause.

The original plan called for a shared gate: rollout to callers would continue only when both sides could be reproduced reliably; if one side was intermittent while the other was normal, it would still count as a failure. On withdrawal, existing samples would stay unchanged; only the approach that "both can be consolidated through the same entry point" would be dropped, returning to separate records. The benefit was that partial success would not offset gaps on the other side; the cost was just as clear: two phenomena with no confirmed common origin would be tied to a single judgment.

## Two candidate approaches

**Keep the combined trial.** Continue treating the string samples and the before/after write states as a single stopping point. The benefit is a simple rollout gate, without reviewers first having to determine where the issue belongs. The drawback is that if the file side does not pass through the value-object entry point, samples will accumulate in the wrong place, and progress on the string side will also be held up.

**Collect separately first.** On the string side, record results only for the chained calls actually made; on the file side, trace entry paths independently from the discovery entry point. The benefit is that each record stays closer to its own subject; the drawback is that a shared gate cannot be provided immediately before the split, and reviewers still have to decide when the two tracks should meet again.

The initial draft chose the former and recorded "stop rollout if either side cannot be reproduced reliably" as a conservative judgment. That choice is retained here; it must not be retroactively recast as a conclusion about `Stringable.php`'s responsibilities.

## The later review

A sample was later attached to HCF-207; the card still required separate records of the visible results of one successful call and one failed call. It supplemented the string-side material, but was not enough to prove a common origin with the file side. HCF-223, in contrast, required a list of the paths actually entered and those ruled out in the temporary repository, starting from the discovery entry point for filesystem atomicity. That requirement exposed exactly what the old trial proposal had left unanswered: this page still does not make clear where observation of the file side should begin.

The old shared gate can therefore still be read as a pause condition, but should not be treated as an attribution of cause. If the samples cannot be reproduced reliably, stopping this trial still makes sense; but "stopping" does not automatically mean the issue has been traced to string wrapping, file writes, or the component split. The initial draft collapsed these layers together, which is the part of this proposal most likely to mislead later readers.

Still unresolved: whether the success and failure samples in HCF-207 cover the same set of chained calls; whether the paths listed in HCF-223 can intersect with this value-object entry point; and, if the two paths remain separate throughout, whether to retain the original shared gate as a conservative release constraint or split the work entirely into two trials. For string samples, see HCF-207; to fill in the file paths, see HCF-223.
