# Troubleshooting Tree for Auxiliary Loading of Legacy Namespaces

This page still retains the troubleshooting entry point from the early stage of component splitting. It is often used to handle two superficially similar situations: the caller says a helper is unavailable when loaded standalone, or a legacy namespace cannot be found at runtime. Both may appear around the split, but they are not the same determination. The old version grouped them together as "loading not complete." That classification is sufficient to help someone locate the file first, but not sufficient to declare that a namespace has been retired.

First, preserve the shortest branch from that time:

```text
The error is near the helper name or function file
|
+-- The call does not go through complete application startup
|   `-- Check standalone helper loading's file loading and declaration visibility
|
+-- The call text still contains the legacy namespace
    `-- Check legacy namespace retirement's name resolution and replacement scope
```

Before entering the branch, retain these three pieces of information exactly as given: the name written by the caller, the location where the problem appeared, and whether application startup had been completed at that location. The third item is not for determining whether the application itself is healthy; it only prevents the standalone loading path and the normal runtime path from being mixed into one record. Without these three pieces of information, do not send the issue directly to namespace migration handling.

The old entry is still `src/utils/src/Functions.php`. The corresponding record points to version `v_prev`. The file header shows:

```php
use Hyperf\Utils\ApplicationContext;
use Hyperf\Utils\Arr;
use Hyperf\Utils\Backoff;
use Hyperf\Utils\Collection;
```

This content is suitable as a starting point for tracing back: it places the function file alongside neighboring objects such as the application context, arrays, backoff, and collections. It does not indicate that any particular helper necessarily reads a container, nor that the old name is converted here. Early troubleshooting once treated the presence of `ApplicationContext` as sufficient evidence, but after several subsequent case reviews, that inference was found to be too broad; the old conclusion is retained below so that no one follows it and directly changes the caller again.

## Standalone Loading Branch

When the symptom is standalone helper loading, the first question is not "Can this helper be used as a replacement?" but "What exactly did the call site receive?" Go through the call site in the following order:

1. Obtain the helper name from the error or call text; do not first substitute a similar name for it.
2. Return to `Functions.php` and confirm whether the name can be matched to a declaration within the file; if it cannot be found, record "not located in file" and do not infer the declaration location from adjacent imports.
3. If it can be located, classify the call site as standalone loading or completed application startup. What is recorded here is the entry form, not whether either category is successful or unsuccessful.
4. If the same name has a problem in only one of the two categories, retain the call snippets and visible diagnostics from both sides, and stop at the loading boundary; do not immediately rewrite it as legacy namespace retirement.
5. If the declaration cannot be located on either side, first check whether the name written by the caller was originally in legacy namespace form, then move to the next branch.

This stop point is important. When the file header contains `ApplicationContext`, the old runbook would have people add the application context first and try again. That action was later not verified as a general recovery measure: it may change the call entry point and thereby mask the standalone loading problem itself. You may still record "change in symptoms after completing application startup" as part of the case record, but you cannot treat it as the helper's normal loading condition.

Another old habit was to see `Arr`, `Backoff`, or `Collection` and trace outward through those objects. This wastes time when the function name is unclear. Now follow up on them only when the call text explicitly involves those objects; otherwise, stop at the helper declaration and its direct call site. This does not deny the relationships of these imports; it simply downgrades them from default clues to name-triggered clues.

### Still-Retained Old Operation

An old record said: "First make the call enter the application container; the helper problem will usually disappear." This sentence reflects an attribution made at the time, not the conclusion after later notes were added to this page. It cannot be used to confirm that the split succeeded, nor to decide that the old name should be deleted. When someone restores a call based on this sentence, attach the names and entry forms before and after the restoration; do not mix the restoration action into the namespace retirement record.

## Legacy Namespace Branch

The starting point for legacy namespace retirement is the actual old name that appears, not a preset replacement table. First retain the complete name from the error, then confirm the object name ultimately requested by the caller. If the name has already changed to the new form but the issue still occurs near the helper file, return to the standalone loading branch; if the caller still writes the old form, only then continue examining the migration impact.

```text
The caller retains the legacy namespace
|
+-- A corresponding new name or call site can be found
|   `-- Record the replacement scope at this location; do not treat other callers as migrated as well
|
+-- No corresponding name can be found
|   `-- Retain the original name and diagnostics, then stop; the replacement relationship cannot be inferred from the import of Functions.php
|
`-- The name has been updated but the helper is still unavailable
    `-- Return to standalone helper loading and check the entry form
```

"Legacy namespace is missing" and "legacy namespace is retired" must also be written separately. The former is only a symptom of one run; the latter requires knowing whether the caller has switched, whether the old name is still being resolved, and whether standalone loading has another issue. This distinction was added to the old runbook later to prevent changing the caller to another helper just because a name could not be found once. No complete replacement list is recorded here, so this cannot be used as the basis for a bulk migration.

If the caller has an old name, the record should include at least: the original name, the call site, and the resolved name or unresolved state. Do not write only "compatibility failed." "Compatibility failed" combines the name problem and the loading problem into one sentence, so later review cannot determine which branch was taken. If the name-resolution result changes with the entry point, do not choose one occurrence as the final answer; this is precisely the case where the boundaries of the two anomalies intersect.

## Why the Initial Draft Mixed Them Together

The initial draft had few field cases, and all problems started near the function file, so it adopted a rough order: complete the application context first, then check the old name, and finally count an unrecovered call as a remnant of the split. The useful part of this order is that it avoids guessing the implementation directly in the caller; the unreliable part is that the first step changes the runtime conditions. It treated the phenomenon of "no longer appearing after completion" as the cause, but did not record whether the names before and after standalone loading were the same.

Later review corrected only this attribution and did not provide a new global migration conclusion. When tracing back, treat the old order as historical case context: it explains why old records often mention helper, container, and namespace together, but it does not mean that the three have a fixed dependency. Especially in records where only the function name is visible, the operation of adding the container first should not overwrite the original call.

## Review Checkpoints

To review an old record, follow both the file and name directions once; there is no need to expand the entire utils area.

- File direction: From `src/utils/src/Functions.php`, locate the declaration corresponding to the name, then check whether the call site belongs to standalone loading.
- Name direction: Starting from the legacy namespace retained at the call site, confirm whether a clear target name can be obtained; if there is no target, retain the unresolved state.
- Cross direction: When the name has changed but the symptom remains, prioritize recording it as a loading-boundary issue; when the old name remains but the loading condition is unclear, prioritize filling in the entry information.

The two directions can produce different results; this is not a recording conflict. One call, Fang Ke, may already have been renamed, yet still not have the file required for standalone loading; another call, Fang Ke, may still use the old name, but have a complete runtime entry. The old version recorded both situations as "unavailable after component splitting," so when citing this page, review the relevant branch as well and do not quote only the old conclusion under the heading.

## Format for On-Call Records

The following format was added later so that the next review would not have to start by guessing from the four characters "loading failed":

```text
Call site:
Call name:
Entry form: Standalone loading / Application startup complete / Unconfirmed
Declaration in file: Located / Not located
Name resolution: Old name still present / Target obtained / Unresolved
Current stop point: Loading boundary / Name migration / Insufficient information
```

Do not write two conclusions in "Current stop point." If both truly exist, write first the one that blocked reproduction earliest, and leave the other in the notes. This ensures that a record of a missing legacy namespace is not erased by an application startup action, and that a helper loading problem is not misrecorded as a completed retirement.

This record has not been turned into a new migration guide. It retains the old path, the overly strong container judgment in the initial draft, and the later review method that separated the two types of symptoms. For migration work involving cache placeholder migration, see DOC-21; do not use the old namespace branch here as a replacement for that migration path.

# Cache Placeholder Migration Procedure

Start the verification at `src/cache/src/Helper/StringHelper.php`, but do not treat the directory containing the file as the new component boundary on its own. Use `internal/hyperf-component-evolution`'s reference relationship with `v_prev` as the basis for determining the target location and actual ownership.

Start in a clean working directory. Capture the current state first and confirm that there are no file changes pending merge; if changes are already present, do not mix them with the migration result. Using the current location of `src/cache/src/Helper/StringHelper.php` as a reference, record the call names and imports related to the cache placeholder. This confirms only the entry point for tracing back, not a complete caller list.

The file header currently shows:


`Str` is a direct dependency on this path. During the migration, first verify whether this helper is still loaded by the original cache entry point, then check whether the callers have been adjusted along with the new namespace or Composer boundary. If only the helper was moved and no corresponding change can be seen in the callers, keep that result as-is; do not treat the directory change as completion of the migration.

## Execution sequence

1. Run the corresponding cache placeholder migration command in a clean working directory.
2. Record the exit code verbatim after the command finishes.

# History of Parallel Failure Evidence

This record preserves an earlier assessment of parallel failure evidence from the 3.0 component split discussion. The starting point was `src/utils/src/Exception/ParallelExecutionException.php`. One option was to take the directory containing `ParallelExecutionException` as its post-split home and continue organizing around the exception type and names such as `results` and `throwable`. This would be quick to organize and keep later lookups in one place, but it would mistake "the exception can be found here" for "this is where responsibility for the exception lies." The other option was to keep this file only as a starting point for checking parallel failures, trace references to confirm who creates the exception and who consumes the results, and then decide whether the namespace and Composer manifest should move with the component. The second option was slower, but it kept exception evidence separate from component responsibility.

The second option was adopted at the time. This record does not assign the path as the final home or interpret a single difference in results as a split failure. This page therefore preserves the decision not to settle the question based on the filename at the time, along with a still somewhat dated starting point for verification. # Managed Channel Cleanup Troubleshooting Tree

Start with the public entry point where the cleanup symptoms appear. Record what the entry point actually returns, or the exception it throws; don't just write "cleanup failed." Verification on this page starts with `src/utils/src/Channel/ChannelManager.php`, corresponding to repository `internal/hyperf-component-evolution` at `v_prev`. The direct dependencies visible in the file header are:

```php
use Hyperf\Engine\Channel;
```

- If the entry point returns a value, keep the full value, then check whether anything in it corresponds to a close or flush operation on a managed channel. If the return value is empty, record that explicitly too; don't treat it as "no channel."
- If the entry point throws an exception, keep the exception type, message, and triggering action. If all you know is "an error was thrown," stop here; don't classify the exception as outside the channel lifecycle.
- If there is neither a return value nor an exception you can record, first confirm whether the entry point actually reached cleanup. If you can't confirm where execution got to, stop; don't keep inferring call relationships from filenames.

## Branch 1: close produces a result, flush does not

First, rerun the existing entry points related to close and flush separately, with only one action per run. If close returns but flush produces no result, record the difference between the two outputs and review the handling location in ChannelManager.php where those two names appear next to each other. Check whether the cleanup result is retained only after flush; without corresponding output, don't change "no result" to "cleaned up."

If both actions complete but the outer layer still reports no cleanup, stop on this path and pass it on for further checking against records that show the outer call. Don't infer which component the consumer belongs to from this file's path.

Keep the first exception; don't overwrite it with a second run. If the exception occurs in close, check whether the same invocation also executed flush. If it did not, record "flush not reached after close" and stop the investigation at close. If flush was still executed, put the order of close and flush, along with each action's output or exception, in the same record, then review the direct use of Channel in the file.

If the exception only appears on repeated cleanup, first compare the return values or exceptions from the first and second invocations. If you can't confirm that the two inputs are identical, don't conclude "caused by repeated calls"; record only the fact that the inputs differ and the items still to be checked.


They indicate that the review should cover both context access and exception paths, but they do not establish that the file is the source of all state changes. The file's directory placement after the split, the proxy object, and the actual callers need to be checked separately. The previous version retained the claim that "abnormal state after passing through the proxy" was directly attributable to Context because there were no counterexamples at the time. We are no longer using that claim to drive batch migration.

Batch by caller first, not by file count. In each batch, change only one entry point confirmed to go through proxy forwarding. Calls outside that entry point continue on the old path. If something goes wrong, this lets us restore a small part of the integration rather than roll back the entire component split.

Use the following routes to compare before and after the split:

```text
Before the split
Caller ──> old entry point ──> proxy forwarding ──> subsequent state read

During the split
Caller ──> new entry point ──> proxy forwarding ──> subsequent state read
             │
             └──Old entry point retained; switch back on errors
```

The "subsequent state read" in the diagram is not a judgment about where the implementation belongs. It is only a checkpoint: confirm the state seen before the proxy, the state seen after forwarding, and whether both still belong to the same call. Confirming only that the new entry point loads does not show that the state is still usable after forwarding.

Run each batch through the following sequence:

- Starting where the caller enters the proxy, record the object and state. Do not include unrelated ordinary calls.
- After switching to the new entry point, confirm that this call still goes through the same forwarding path. If it does not, treat it as an entry-point migration failure first; do not conflate it with a state issue.
- Check the state after forwarding. If the issue appears only here, retain the records from before and after the proxy, and examine the implementation in `CoroutineProxy.php` adjacent to `Context` and `RuntimeException`.
- If an exception branch is taken or the objects do not match, switch this caller back to the old entry point. Do not remove the old entry point until the batch has been verified.

Here, "switch back" only means restoring this caller's original integration; it does not mean rolling back the entire component split. Other calls Fang Ke may already be running stably through the new entry point during the split. Reverting them too would wipe out migration results that were working and remove the comparison point for the next review.

A counterexample was later added to HCF-214. The card originally only described abnormal state after proxy forwarding and asked the relevant maintainer to check the current behavior and entry points for further investigation. Once the counterexample was added, "look at Context first; the problem should be right here" could no longer be used as a conclusion. At a minimum, it shows that this first place to look cannot rule out entry-point changes, the relationship between objects before and after the proxy, or exception branches.

The card was then reassigned to the person on duty because the previous owner was not involved in this cycle. This change is retained here to show that the review had not established a complete implementation-level explanation at that point, not to treat a change of responsibility as a technical conclusion. The migration record should include the names of the calls actually checked and the recovery actions taken; it must not just say "reviewed."

The previous version's "check Context first" is still useful as an initial navigation step, especially when the call has indeed entered `CoroutineProxy.php`, but it is no longer a migration acceptance criterion. Acceptance must be based on a specific batch of calls: the new entry point does not bypass forwarding, the state after forwarding does not show the issue under review, and no exception path is taken that requires restoring the old entry point.

If any of these cannot be confirmed, keep that batch on the old entry point. Do not remove the compatibility path early just to finish the directory split. Once the relationship between the callers and the proxy has been clarified, decide whether to proceed with the next batch.

# Proxy Forwarding Migration Process

This page is still being referenced, but it documents the migration approach used during component split, not a general explanation of all proxy issues that came later. The earliest approach treated the proxy as a continuous channel: once the caller switched to the new entry point, it would still pass through forwarding, so the state should remain visible as before. That approach was suitable for breaking changes into small batches, but it compressed "state anomaly" into a single-point problem.

Later field feedback required us to correct this. An anomaly occurring after forwarding does not mean that it was caused solely by `src/utils/src/Traits/CoroutineProxy.php`, `Context`, or by a single proxy action. This file remains an entry point that can currently be read further, but it can only lead the investigation to adjacent implementations; it cannot assign attribution among the caller, state object, and exception path.

During the split, the two paths need to coexist for some time: the old entry point handles calls that have not yet been confirmed, while the new entry point handles calls that have completed local checks. Migration is complete not when the old directory is no longer referenced, but when a particular caller, under the new entry point, has passed through proxy forwarding and its state and exception behavior have been reviewed separately. Without this comparison, the old entry point cannot be deleted.

## Early Approach on Record

The first version made the checking order very narrow: start by looking at `Context`, then find the branches of `RuntimeException`; once the state was wrong after forwarding, restore the old entry point. This order came from the dependencies visible in the file header:

```php
use Hyperf\Context\Context;
use RuntimeException;
```

This is still useful because the two names keep the reading scope to the direct neighbors of `CoroutineProxy.php`. The problem is that it makes people skip two earlier checks: whether the call actually entered the proxy, and whether the entry point after migration is still for the same type of call. Looking only at these two dependencies misrecords "did not enter forwarding," "entered a different object," and "reached an exception branch after entry" as the same kind of state problem.

The route in the old record is retained below. It shows where the before-and-after comparison was made at the time; it does not indicate fixed ownership at the code level.

```text
Before split
caller ──> old entry point ──> proxy forwarding ──> state read

After split, a batch under verification
caller ──> new entry point ──> proxy forwarding ──> state read
             │
             └──old entry point can still be restored
```

The incorrect wording at the time was: as long as the new entry point could still reach the proxy, migration could continue. This wording is deprecated. Reaching the proxy only shows that the entry point has not been completely disconnected; it does not show that the state still exists in the same way before and after the proxy, nor that no exception handling was triggered.

## Move a Batch of Calls from the Old Entry Point

The unit of migration is always the caller, not the trait file and not a one-time directory replacement. First find one caller known to pass through proxy forwarding; keep the other calls at the old entry point. This way, if verification fails, the access path that can be restored is that of this one caller, and the already migrated parts will not be mixed back into the problem.

Before starting, record the following items for the batch:

- Where the call enters the old entry point; if the entry point is only guessed from its name, stop first and do not record the guess as the migration target.
- Which caller the new entry point is intended to handle. The same proxy name does not mean the same entry point.
- What state is visible before the proxy. There is no need to copy all irrelevant context; record only enough to compare it with the state after the proxy.
- Whether the state is still accessible after the proxy; if an anomaly appears, whether it occurred before entering the proxy, during forwarding, or after forwarding.
- Whether the old entry point can still be restored for this caller. If the old entry point has already been cleaned up in the same batch, first restore a comparable path and then continue checking.

The first item has a very practical purpose. During component split, the most common problem is not that the proxy file disappears, but that the caller switches to the new directory and no longer takes the original forwarding path. If the entry location is not confirmed, all subsequent reading concerning `Context` and `RuntimeException` may be looking at code that this call never executed.

The second item prevents a directory change from being treated as functionally equivalent. The new entry point can load and the caller can continue running, but it may no longer pass through the same proxy. At that point, the observation should not be recorded as "state anomaly after forwarding"; more accurately, the entry relationship for this batch has not yet been verified, and the old entry point remains in place.

The third and fourth items need to be recorded as a pair. Early notes required only checking the state after forwarding; later experience showed that this was insufficient: without a reference from before the proxy, it is impossible to distinguish state that was already unavailable from a change that appeared only after forwarding. The record does not need to expand into a dump of the entire call chain; the focus is the difference before and after the proxy for the same call, and whether it entered an exception branch.

The fifth item is the migration safety line. The old entry point exists not to maintain two implementations long term, but to provide a comparable object to return to when the current batch encounters a problem. A caller without a restoration path should not be put in the first batch, nor should it be allowed through based on the results of other calls that are already stable.

## Classification After the Counterexample

The original observation left by HCF-214 was that the state was anomalous after proxy forwarding. The card required the maintainer of the corresponding module to verify the current version's behavior and identify an entry point for further checking. The counterexample added later forced us to retract the claim that "checking Context first is enough to locate the issue."

The counterexample did not automatically provide complete attribution. It was only enough to disprove one premature way of proceeding: we cannot attribute all anomalies to context reads merely because `CoroutineProxy.php` introduced `Hyperf\Context\Context`; nor can the presence of `RuntimeException` in the file header justify concluding that every anomaly has already entered a clear failure branch. The two dependencies are a starting point for reading, not a migration result.

The card was later reassigned to the current on-call person, with the reason recorded that the previous owner was not available in this cycle. This history shows that someone needed to continue supplementing the field findings at the time, but it does not show that implementation-level confirmation was completed afterward. The wording "actually reviewed once" in the old version should also be understood within this scope: it means that a migration relationship and a counterexample were reviewed, not that the entire proxy chain had been confirmed.

After the counterexample, the recording method was changed to first write the three result types separately:

1. The new entry point did not reach forwarding. This is an entry-point migration misalignment; after restoring the old entry point, verify the entry relationship first.
2. The new entry point reached forwarding, but the state seen before and after the proxy was different. This is retained as a candidate state anomaly, and checking needs to continue along the direct neighbors of `CoroutineProxy.php`.
3. The new entry point reached forwarding, but the state comparison could not be completed, or an exception path was encountered. This result cannot be recorded as passed; keep the old entry point and complete the before-and-after record for this call.

The three result types look similar, but the recovery actions differ. The first cannot be resolved by checking context dependencies; the second cannot omit the comparison before the proxy; and the third cannot continue deleting the compatibility entry just because it has not been reproduced consistently. The old record combined them into "state anomaly after proxy processing," which is exactly why this page later still needed to retain a revision trail.

## What to Leave When Restoring the Old Path

When an inconsistency appears, first restore the caller where the problem occurred to the old entry point. Do not roll back the entire component split, and do not casually change the other new entry points back. Other batches may not have the same entry relationship; a full rollback both expands the changes and loses the comparable migration state.

After restoration, write down at least two pieces of information that can be reviewed later: whether this call entered forwarding at the old entry point and at the new entry point, respectively, and where the state anomaly or exception branch appeared. If it is not even possible to answer whether the call entered forwarding, record only that the entry point has not been confirmed; do not fill it in as Context having become invalid or the proxy object having been replaced.

Completion of the restoration does not mean that the old entry point is kept permanently. It only moves this batch from "in split" back to "pending verification." The next time work continues, start from the caller's entry location; do not continue guessing directly in `CoroutineProxy.php`. The file path is a reading entry point, not a substitute for field evidence.

There was previously a shortcut: clean up the old entry point first, then wait for the new entry point to expose a problem before adding a compatibility layer. This approach is no longer used. It turns a problem that could originally have been compared before and after into recovery work, and it cannot distinguish whether the old path had the same state to begin with. A call whose old entry point was removed this way cannot be marked as migration complete merely because the new entry point appears normal; first recover a comparable old access relationship, or leave the call unconfirmed.

## Materials Still Usable as Entry Points

`CoroutineProxy.php` is the source-code entry point that can still be opened. `Context` and `RuntimeException` in the file header are clearly visible adjacency information; how the specific state is obtained, how exceptions are thrown, and which callers necessarily pass through the trait still need to be confirmed in references for the corresponding revision.

HCF-214 are useful for referring back to the exception description and the counterexample notes added at the time. They should not be treated as a migration checklist: the card only required checking the current version's behavior and identifying an entry point; it did not make a determination for every caller. Materials related to gRPC pool integration are in DOC-27, and should not be mixed with this page's proxy forwarding migration.

The smallest sequence still usable now is: choose one caller, keep the old entry point, confirm whether it enters forwarding, and compare the state before and after the proxy; if an anomaly appears or the comparison does not hold, restore this batch and write down where it stopped. Compared with the early "check Context first" sequence, this one adds entry-point confirmation and also retains the old path as the comparison object.

The items still not clarified are which callers should continue to pass through this forwarding after the split, and which of them no longer depend on the old entry point. They cannot be inferred from the two dependencies in the file header. Future notes should be attached directly beside the migration record for the specific call; do not again merge all unconfirmed callers into one general state anomaly.

# database Caller Dual-State Postmortem

This postmortem preserves an anomaly that was very narrow in scope, but could easily be obscured by later pages. When replaying real call samples centered on example, the same object showed two states at different save points. The earliest draft did not place it in any single failure category, describing it only as "the same object shows two states"; no subsequent root-cause explanation was sufficient to replace the original record. As a result, the early provisional assessment, recovery page, rollback checks, and later-added card actions remain recorded side by side in the order they appeared.

"State" here is not an overall characterization of the entire database component. It refers to an inconsistency between the entry page and the old record for a real call sample built around example in database · Client Integration. The adaptation boundary and integration feedback need to be revisited because of this, but the existing materials do not classify each of them as affected or unaffected.

The phrase most likely to be misread is "current revision". At each of the two save points, the page was shown as current, but they did not show the same content. This wording indicates only the text displayed on the page when it was saved; it does not prove that the two sets of materials came from the same build, the same request context, or the same call path. The early records also did not preserve a sufficiently continuous chain of version relationships, so the word "current" cannot be used to infer which overwrote which.

## The Initially Captured State

The early draft was incomplete, with one timestamp still left blank, but several observations in it should be preserved together with the original sample:

- The replay used an existing real call sample, not a similar input reconstructed for the investigation.
- The first visible difference was that the middleware pipe did not match the old record.
- The entry point showed different current revisions at the two save points.
- The decision at the time was to preserve the input and page versions and stop retrying.
- In subsequent checks, typed AST could be restored; the change in the gRPC pool was not explained.

These observations do not form a complete causal chain. The fact that the middleware pipe was noticed first does not mean it changed first, much less that it was the only cause. The draft placed it under "first observed", and someone later interpreted that sentence as meaning the adaptation boundary had already changed. That interpretation was not confirmed; it is preserved to retain the context for stopping retries at the time, not to elevate it to the final attribution.

> Earlier assessment: the middleware pipe differs from the old record, so the adaptation boundary may have changed.
>
> Later note: typed AST can be restored, but why the gRPC pool changed is still unknown.

The first sentence was later dropped as a causal explanation. It relied on a single comparison and did not explain the differences between the two current revisions. The second sentence did not classify the incident as a gRPC pool failure either, only stating that after the recovery of typed AST was observed, some state changes still remained unexplained. Taken together, the two sentences show where the early investigation stalled: there was already a recoverable object, but no material to tie the remaining differences together.

An early version also retained "Missing timestamp: ____". This blank entry should be preserved. The existing records allow the order of observations to be reconstructed, but not the exact times; filling in the blank to create a seemingly complete timeline would mislead later readers into thinking that the on-call staff had kept a continuous record that never existed.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Actual call sample
    participant E as Current entry point
    participant R as Original record
    participant P as Recovery page
    S->>E: Replay example
    E-->>R: middleware pipe differs from the old record
    R-->>P: Original failure window remains preserved
    P-->>S: typed AST can be recovered
```

The diagram only represents the adjacency relationships in the records. It does not mean that the recovery page was generated directly from the original record, nor that the recovery of typed AST explained the divergence in entry-point state. The pages are arranged in sequence to show that they were all retained in connection with the same sample; the causal relationships among them remain unconfirmed.

## Handling sequence that can be reconstructed

The draft does not contain a reliable minute-by-minute sequence, but the following order can be reconstructed.

1. The object in the actual call sample for example was found to differ from the old record.
2. The difference in middleware pipe was noted and provisionally treated as a lead pointing toward the adaptation boundary.
3. The original input and the version retained by `docs/adj-database/incidents/database-client-integration-two-states-for-one-object.md` were saved.
4. Further retries were stopped, and new entry-point results were no longer allowed to replace the original state.
5. Subsequent checks showed that typed AST could be recovered, while the differences in the gRPC pool remained unexplained.

Step five cannot be used to infer that the first four steps had already been resolved. The recovery of typed AST was a later, limited observation, not a corrected version of the early incident record. The early materials contained neither continuous request-level records nor a set of saved relationships that could reliably order the two current revisions, so this retrospective records only "what was seen first, what was retained afterward, and what was added later," and does not state an unrecorded start time or a time of complete recovery.

At the save entry point, the on-site response prioritized retaining the old link and page content. This preserved the appearance of the state, but also left an obvious gap: there was only a screenshot-like retelling, which still could not explain why the other path appeared normal. The page's appearance cannot pin down the replay context or provide the relationship between the two versions. This deficiency is inherent in the old record itself and cannot be turned into a confirmed version investigation merely by adding a paragraph of description later.

## What each of the two states left behind

The original record, the other save point at the entry, the recovery page, and the later-added check cannot be collapsed into a single "correct version." They answer different questions.

| Material | Content retained at the time | Role in the event |
|---|---|---|
| Original record | Initial deviation, old input, and middleware pipe differed from the old record | Starting point of the failure window |
| Other save point at the entry | The same object was displayed in a different state, and another current revision appeared | A state fork was observed |
| Recovery page | typed AST can be recovered | Partial recovery observation |
| Later-added check | `rollback_checked` | Rollback state was checked |

The original record cannot be overwritten by the recovery page. The former shows what differed from the old materials during a replay, while the latter only shows that at least one object could be recovered afterward. Keeping only the recovery page would give readers the impression that the state had never diverged; keeping only the original record would omit the recovery observation that appeared later. The two materials are kept side by side; later page content is not backfilled into the initial incident.

"Recovery" in the table does not mean that "all callers have been recovered." The only thing currently supported by the record is that typed AST can be recovered. Actual caller samples, adaptation boundaries, integration feedback, and exit criteria are adjacent subjects of the same joint integration effort, but they do not automatically share conclusions merely because they fall within the same scope. This anomaly was first observed at middleware pipe; that does not justify concluding that all integration feedback came from the same change.

Both pages displayed the current revision, which is precisely the source of this misreading. If the later-saved page is called the sole current version, the original failure window will be seen as an old state; if the earliest page is treated as the sole baseline, the later recovery observation will instead be mistakenly deemed invalid. The existing materials support only "the two save points differed at the time they were saved"; they do not support assigning them an authoritative order in which one can replace the other.

## Reason and cost of stopping retries

Stopping retries was not a judgment that the problem no longer existed; it was a damage-control action at the scene. The object had already shown different states at the two save points; if the same entry were refreshed repeatedly, the next result would still be displayed by the page as current. This would produce more results, but blur what exactly had been seen during the initial replay.

The cost of this decision should also be kept on record. Once work stopped, the early draft lacked a continuous series of samples and could not establish whether the state change was a one-off or would recur in other call samples. The draft's constraint that "unrecorded actions must not be filled in with speculation" still applies here: retries that were not preserved cannot be written up in the postmortem as verification that was performed; request relationships that were not preserved likewise cannot be used to state that a particular path had been ruled out.

At the time, the description of the "adaptation boundary" was also too broad. Actual call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback are closely related during integration testing, but they are not the same thing. A difference in the middleware pipe can show that the old record and the replay differ, but it cannot show that the same kind of change occurred at every adaptation point. The point of preserving the original failure window is to prevent the recovery page from erasing this distinction.

An early secondhand account treated "the other path is normal" as a reason to downplay the anomaly. It did not preserve enough information about version relationships and replay context, so it cannot serve as counterevidence. Another path appearing normal proves neither that the original sample had no problem nor that the two states were compatible to begin with. This page records only the limitations of that account and does not expand it into specific requests or user scenarios that were never preserved.

## Explanations We Once Leaned Toward, Then Abandoned

### middleware pipe is the only cause

This was the earliest working hypothesis, with only one piece of direct evidence: it differed from the old record. This hypothesis quickly ran into two problems. First, the entry point's current revision already differed between the two saved checkpoints, and looking only at the middleware pipe could not explain how the states diverged. Second, typed AST could be restored, while the change in the gRPC pool remained unexplained. These two subsequent observations only show that the initial focus was too narrow, not that the middleware pipe was never involved.

Therefore, "possibly a change in the adaptation boundary" in the old draft is retained as the assessment made at the time, but it is no longer used to frame subsequent conclusions. The available material does not show that this change was confirmed, nor that it was completely ruled out. Deleting it would obscure why the investigation stopped here at the time; presenting it as the root cause would go beyond what the original record can support.

### The recovery page means the incident is over

After the recovery page appeared, it was easy to rewrite "typed AST can be restored" as a claim that the entire object had recovered. The material does not provide enough support for that claim. Recovery was seen in one explicitly recorded observation; the questions of why the two states coexisted, why the gRPC pool changed, and how large the impact window was remain unanswered. A later review separated the observation of recovery from root cause confirmation to avoid presenting a single green result as the end of the incident.

This correction does not negate the value of the recovery page. The recovery page shows that the investigation did not stop at the failed sample, and it should not be excluded from the original record either. Its limitation is that the page did not preserve relationships linking the recovery actions, the current revision, and the original differences on an item-by-item basis. The recovery page can show "what was observed later", but it cannot replace the investigation into "why things differed in the first place".

### A single rollback check is enough to explain the recovery

There is one explicit action in the later material: HCFA-012 records `rollback_checked`. This only shows that someone checked the rollback-related status, not that a rollback was definitely performed, how far it progressed, or whether a rollback restored typed AST. The old records do not preserve this causal link, so the action on the card cannot be expanded into "recovery completed through rollback."

This explanation needs to be called out separately because the rollback check appears in later material, and readers can easily treat it as following the stopping of retries in the early draft. The two actions did not occur at the same time. The early version knew only about preserving the state at the time and stopping refreshes; it did not know about the later rollback check or the subsequent assignee changes.

## Handoff traces left by actions added later

After the rollback check in HCFA-012, the assignee changed in the records, with the stated reason being that the original owner had moved on to handle a production incident and others would continue following up. This shows that observations of recovery and the investigation into the cause were not documented as a continuous sequence in the same section of the records. # database Call Path Proposal

This compares two integration paths for `database-client-integration`. The first would continue using `serializer hook`, placing the changes callers need near the existing serialization hook; the second would split out `atomic filesystem` as another entry point with a clear boundary. Both paths are still at the proposal stage, with no start date, and neither has been written up as an integration rule already in effect.

## Differences between the two entry points

The advantage of `serializer hook` is that changes stay localized, and existing callers don't have to migrate to a new entry point right away. The objections are also straightforward: it ties writing files to disk to serialization timing. Callers see the same hook, but don't necessarily face the same failure handling. When a failure occurs, some paths need to return to the serialization stage; others need to handle cases where a file has already been written but subsequent actions are incomplete. Continuing to use it would mean smaller changes in the short term, but for `legacy retirement`, it's hard to tell from a single hook whether any callers remain.

`atomic filesystem`, on the other hand, separates out file operations. Success, failure, and rollback actions can then be assessed near the file entry point, and failure exits are easier to match to caller integration-testing records. The trade-off is that existing consumers need to reconfirm the entry point. Callers that relied on the timing of `serializer hook` cannot assume compatibility will carry over; if `nested configuration` is still expanded through the old path, which side it belongs on after the split will also need a separate decision.

## Trial scope and rollback points

The preference is to put `atomic filesystem` forward as the path to trial first, without recording that preference as a final decision. The trial only covers database call samples where the call entry point, input file, and failure exit can be clearly identified. If it's unclear whether a caller still relies on the old timing, keep the sample for now and don't count it as an old caller eligible for retirement.

There are two rollback conditions: first, the trial produces failure exits that cannot be distinguished, leaving callers to guess the state again; second, callers still in use are found to be able to perform their original actions only through `serializer hook`. If either condition is triggered, roll back to the entry point used before the change and retain a pre-change routing snapshot. It has not yet been decided here whether rollback should only restore the old entry point or also clean up the file writes already made; this needs to be checked against each caller still in use.

## What's still unresolved

- The list of callers still using `legacy retirement` has not yet been compiled.
- Where `nested configuration` belongs after the split is undecided.
- Whether rollback should restore only the old entry point is undecided.
- Validation of reverse inputs in the trial window is not yet complete.

Related materials can be found at `docs/adj-database/proposals/rejected-database-client-integration-approach.md`. If implementation conditions change later, a new version should be added to document the path actually used; this page retains the comparison, objections, and rollback points for the approach not adopted this time.

# di Compatibility Catalog Approach Proposal

This approach was ultimately not selected for adoption. The value of keeping this record is not to prove that `component boundary` is better, but to bring together why we wanted to try it at the time, what did not work, and under what conditions it should be rolled back. The old entry point remains one of the options being compared, and separating out `review evidence` remains only a candidate design; neither can be treated as the catalog rules in effect based on this record alone.

## What the draft actually compared

Continuing with the `gRPC pool` approach offered existing record-keeping practices and a shorter path to change. The objections focused elsewhere: if review evidence remained attached to the same object, `namespace ownership`, input sources, and conclusions could easily move together, making it hard later to tell which parts were catalog facts and which were just material left over from a single review.

Separating out `review evidence` would let catalog objects and review materials change independently. The costs of this split were also clear: ownership of `container identity` would need to be reconfirmed, we would need to know whether `channel lifecycle` was an object property or the process of a single run, and we would have to accept the old entry point and the new boundary coexisting for a while. Early drafts presented the split as relatively safe, but that was only a working assumption, with no trial results to support it.

`typed AST` was considered as a possible implementation direction, but no commitment was made to it as part of this approach. It might change the shape of the catalog's inputs, but it could not by itself answer who owned the objects, how the old entry point would be rolled back, or why the two environments produced different results. `autoload file` was also just one piece of material still to be investigated, not a confirmed catalog boundary.

## Stop conditions recorded in the trial draft

The original plan was a small, two-week trial: one group would continue using `unadopted-di-compatibility-catalog-approach`, while the other would try `component boundary`. Both groups were to use the same users, inputs, and observation window, changing only the way the catalog was organized. Without feedback from real users, or with only a single green result, the trial would not count as a success. If locating issues did not get faster, the number of misjudgments did not fall, or `namespace ownership` could not be restored on exit, the candidate entry point was to be rolled back.

Rolling back did not mean deleting the old material. The old entry point, raw inputs, and first visible result all had to be retained, so that the cleaned-up state after a failure would not be mistaken for the state before the trial. If the candidate approach went beyond the interface in place, further expansion was to stop; it had not been decided at the time which party would cover that gap, so this record does not assign ownership to anyone who had not been confirmed.

## The execution window provided no answer

# Runtime observability entry point migration process

`docs/adj-view-engine/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md` is the entry point for the view engine runtime observability console's migration records. The paths collected here are for finding runtime signals, failure context, and recovery observation windows, not for giving the page directory a new name. Each record must still lead back to the original material; the replacement location supports a verified path, rather than being an explanatory page with a similar title.

This index lists only three types of objects: old entry points, replacement locations, and callers that still go through the old entry points. Putting all three on the same row is for planning the switchover, not to indicate that they are already equivalent. The old entry point preserves the original records; the replacement location retains the destination confirmed to be reachable; the caller identifies who actually still enters through the old path. Descriptions that cannot be traced back remain on the old entry point side, marked as outdated, and are not merged just because the index has a new row.

```text
Old entry point ──Preserve original records──> Migration index ──Point after verification──> Replacement location
  ▲                         │
  └────── Roll back current batch ─────┘

Caller ──Enter via its own directory or report──> Original record for the current revision
```

The arrows in the diagram describe migration arrangements, not a decommissioning notice. The old entry point remains readable during the switchover, and the replacement location does not automatically become a recovery point simply because it has been entered in the index. Each caller may enter only through its own existing directory or report; it must not use another path with a similar name to fill in the records further along its path.

## How to write migration rows

Whenever you prepare to move an object, start from the old entry point. State where the runtime observability materials used to be accessed, and confirm that the original records can still be opened. Do not turn the old entry point's content into a summary and then delete it; the failure context and recovery observation window must remain alongside the original records. If the old entry point itself is no longer accessible, record that state in the index; this is separate from "the replacement location does not yet support the path."

Next, fill in the replacement location. Only an address actually reached from the original record can be used as a replacement location. New categories in the directory, pages with similar names, and destinations inferred from display text may only be kept as candidates and cannot replace the original path. The migration index records an entry point relationship that can be retraced, not the result of organizing a directory.

Finally, enter the caller. The caller is not a generic list of users, but the specific path that will actually switch from the old entry point to the replacement location in this batch. If a caller still enters through the old entry point, keep the old entry point. Even if a caller can open the replacement location, the row cannot be marked as migrated if the original record cannot be traced back to the current revision.

Early drafts compared continuing along `component boundary` with splitting out `autoload file` separately. The two sections had different failure exits, which is why they were not written as a single migration line at the time. This judgment is only for keeping the two sets of records separate; subsequent verification must still start from their respective callers, and the results from one side must not be applied to the other.

## Move only one caller per batch

For each batch, select one caller that is still in use. During the switchover, change only the link that takes this caller from the index to the replacement location, keep the old entry point accessible, and do not move the original records. This keeps any observed problems traceable to the same route, rather than letting them be obscured by the directory state after bulk changes.

After the switchover, first check whether the caller can still see the runtime signals previously associated with it. Then trace back from the failure context to confirm that the original record remains available within the recovery observation window. If either of these two links is broken, roll back this caller's link. The replacement location may remain, and so may the recorded failure location; rolling back does not mean erasing the trail.

At the end of a batch, the index row only needs to record its own state: whether the caller has moved to the replacement location, whether fallback to the old entry point is still possible, and whether a first point where progress was blocked has been encountered. If the caller has not yet been confirmed, explicitly mark it as pending confirmation. The replacement location's presence in the directory does not substitute for this verification.

Do not rearrange other rows in the same batch. Successfully traversing one path only means that this caller's entry point relationship has been checked; it does not prove that other consumers have migrated, nor that adjacent old entry points can be retired. Keeping the scope to one row makes it possible to see later which switchover affected which recovery records.

## Trace-back checks for the current revision

HCFD-002 provides navigation for verifying an actual consumer's chain at the current revision. During the review, start from that consumer's existing directory or report, follow the actual entry point to the original record, then check whether the replacement location supports the same path. If progress is blocked along the way, record the first point where it stops. Do not rewrite the failure as a generic migration anomaly, and do not fill in missing segments from another path that has already been traversed successfully.

"Verified" in the index only means that this row has completed this trace-back check. It does not mean that all materials have migrated, much less that the old entry point can be deleted. Whether to continue maintaining the old entry point depends on whether this row's caller, original record, and recovery observation window are still usable, not on the amount of green or the number of new names in the index.

HCFD-009 retains a comparison of neighboring paths at the current revision. This comparison is used only to find the first path difference: choose an adjacent path that can be traversed successfully and compare it with the path awaiting migration to find their earliest divergence. Entry points after that divergence cannot be inferred from this. From their first difference onward, the two paths remain in their respective rows, each awaiting review by its own caller.

## Do not flatten time records

`view-engine-operations-observability` is the name used on this page to classify runtime observability materials. It is not the original location of the failure context, nor does it mean that the index update time is the time when the runtime event occurred. Keep the index time, runtime event time, and execution record time separately; record their relationships in the corresponding row when they can be confirmed, and preserve the differences when they cannot.

HCFD-004 retains a case where the same execution record has two timestamp values, 14:32 and 14:47. Keep both times, without choosing one to overwrite the other for now. The later value cannot prove that the replacement location has become stable, and the earlier value does not imply that the old entry point has already become invalid. This row may continue with limited-scope path verification, but must not be included in a batch for retiring old entry points.

When similar time discrepancies arise, first note whether the time refers to a runtime event, an index update, or an execution record. If the three cannot be aligned, continue retaining these timestamps side by side in the recovery observation window. What needs to be preserved here is the differences needed to review the failure context later, not a single sequence created by reorganizing inconsistent records.

If an index row contains an unresolved time discrepancy, do not obscure it with later directory changes. The caller Fang Ke remains at the old entry point, and the replacement location may remain a candidate; however, a retirement decision must wait until the time relationships in that row can be traced back, or the row must be explicitly retained as an outdated record that cannot be traced back.

## Rollback path

Roll back the current batch if any of the following occurs: the replacement location cannot lead back to the original record; the caller cannot see the runtime signals previously associated with it; only an organized summary of the failure context remains; or the index time cannot be matched to the execution record. Limit the rollback to the current caller's route through the old entry point, without deleting the replacement location or overwriting the first failure location already recorded.

After rolling back, first follow the old entry point back to the original record and confirm that the old path is still readable, then leave the caller in the old entry point column. If the old path is already inaccessible, do not designate the replacement location as a recovery point by default. The index must retain both the fact that the old path is unreadable and the fact that the replacement location does not yet support the path, to avoid treating the two failures as a single cause next time.

New material appearing in the recovery observation window must still be recorded close to its original location. A rollback can restore the caller's access route, but it cannot erase path differences that have already occurred. For the next batch, select another caller that is still in use, rather than generalizing this batch's rollback result into a conclusion about all entry points.

HCFD-007 records the temporary handover arrangement for the current migration operation. It covers only this batch's switchover and rollback, and does not mean that the runtime observability console has a long-term maintainer. Therefore, requests to delete an old entry point, merge two historical records, or change the retention period must remain on hold at the corresponding index row, to be handled only after a maintenance arrangement can be confirmed.

## Criteria for retiring the old entry point

Before maintenance of an old entry point is stopped for a row, all four conditions for that row must be met: the replacement location can actually be reached from the original record; each listed caller has migrated or been explicitly rolled back; the failure context in the recovery observation window can still be reviewed; and the row has no unresolved time discrepancies. These conditions apply only to this row and cannot be extrapolated to entry points with similar names.

The navigation in HCFD-012 requires tracing back along the revision of `view-engine-operations-observability` to the earliest reconstructible source. Do this before retiring the old entry point. If the earliest source can only be guessed from the page's display text, continue retaining the old entry point as an outdated record. Outdated means that the replacement location has not yet been shown to support this path, not that the materials no longer need to be reviewed.

At the end of the index, list callers that have migrated separately from callers that remain at the old entry point. Select one of the latter for the next batch and recheck the original record, replacement location, and recovery observation window. HCFD-002, HCFD-004, HCFD-007, HCFD-009, and HCFD-012 can be used to locate chain verification, coexisting timestamps, temporary handover, the first difference, and the earliest source, respectively; the cards serve only as navigation into these records.

# Documentation Site Dual-State Postmortem

At two different viewing times, the entry point for the same object showed different values for the current revision. The documentation site is not a single page: docs, guide, release notes, and records of how expired content was handled each provide their own material, and the entry point also has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. The original record and the recovery page were not merged into a single "current state", because they preserve snapshots from different times.

## Snapshots Preserved Over Time

The first thing observed was that the entry point display did not match the old record, and a difference in coroutine state was recorded at the same time. There was not enough material then to determine whether this was caused by page generation, collection, or some earlier state change. The action taken was straightforward: first save the entry point version and the original record, then stop retrying. Further retries would produce new page results, making the earlier differences harder to compare.

Later, one page showed that nested configuration could be restored. That result only showed that the recovery page had returned to a usable state at that point, not why the two entry points had previously differed. The change in serializer hook also remained unexplained. Placing these two matters side by side in v1 could give the mistaken impression that the recovery had already accounted for the cause; this version still retains the original wording, but puts it back into the sequence of observations.

The scope of impact was not fully quantified. What can be confirmed is that the entry point for the same object presented different values for the current revision at two points in time; this does not imply that all docs or guide content changed at the same time. The original record and the recovery page were kept separately specifically to avoid presenting a partial recovery as confirmation that the entire documentation site was now consistent.

## Timeline

| Time | Record | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial comparison | The entry point state differed from the old record, with a difference in coroutine state | Saved the original record and entry point version, and stopped retrying |
| Subsequent check | nested configuration could be restored | Kept the recovery page without overwriting the initial record |
| 2026-03-30 | HCFE-006 was recorded as `release_classified`; HCFE-007 was recorded as `risk_reviewed` | Continued reviewing the two records separately |
| 2026-03-31 | A later record for HCFE-007 stated that only screenshots remained, and the original request associated with the exit entry point had not been attached | Did not use screenshots to fill in the request conditions |
| After 2026-04-09 | HCFE-013 began addressing inconsistent entry point collection states | Check separately whether collection and execution are enabled |

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant P as Access entry point
    participant R as Original record
    participant V as Recovery page
    U->>P: View the same object
    P->>R: Save the initial state and entry point version
    P-->>V: A recoverable state appears later
    R-->>U: Preserve the initial difference
```

In this timeline, the card actions are later records, not proof that the initial anomaly had been resolved. `release_classified` and `risk_reviewed` only indicate that the relevant records were categorized or reviewed, and did not restore the original request. The later note from HCFE-007, "Only screenshots remain; the original request associated with the exit entry point was not attached", locates the gap at the request level: screenshots can preserve the text visible on the page at the time, but cannot show what conditions applied to the request, nor align the time the page was displayed with the time the record was written.

## How the Earlier Assessment Was Overturned

Originally, placing "nested configuration can be restored" before "still don't know about serializer hook" reflected the order of the observations, not an investigation finding. After recovery, there was still no evidence linking serializer hook to the difference between the two revision values. Their appearance together in one record only indicates that they were noticed together at the time, and does not establish a causal chain.

coroutine state was also an observation, not an attribution of cause. It was enough to prompt the person on duty to save the originals and stop retrying, but without the original request and retrievable complete logs, it could not establish which layer had a problem, whether entry point collection, release notes, or documentation site generation. The older version placed it at the beginning because it was observed first; this addendum has not elevated it to a root cause.

The term "current revision" makes two points in time look like the same moment. In fact, each page claimed to be current, but the records did not provide the full conditions of the two views. The available material also does not establish which revision value was closer to the actual state, so the term used at the time is retained here, without assigning it a correct value.

A later record for HCFE-006 also noted that an expiration action had been sent to the wrong card and was not from the same incident as "on-call handoff amqp · Documentation Portal supplemental entry". This distinction is important: that expiration action cannot be linked to the entry point state change, nor can it be used to fill the gap in the timeline. It only shows that information had previously been incorrectly combined across cards.

## Screenshots, Requests, and Collection State

The screenshots preserved so far support only the claim that "two states were observed". Screenshots cannot recover the original request associated with the exit entry point, nor can they reconstruct the version, context, or execution conditions carried by the request. The original record and entry point version remain valuable, but they cannot answer questions at the request level.

The local description for HCFE-013 requires checking first whether collection and execution are enabled; when there is no evidence for the current entry point, do not fill in zeros. This line of checking belongs to the follow-up records on inconsistent entry point collection states, and cannot retrospectively serve as a complete explanation for this anomaly. Having no record and having confirmed that something did not happen are not the same thing.

The blank item from v1 must also be retained here:

> Missing point in time: ____

The later record dated 2026-03-31 explains that the relevant job has expired, and its logs cannot be retrieved for now. Consequently, this blank has not been filled with a date or a guess. What can be done now is to distinguish where the materials fall in time, not to reconstruct the missing original request.

## Boundaries After Recovery

The recovery page only records that nested configuration can be restored. It did not overwrite the initial entry point state, did not prove that serializer hook had recovered, and certainly did not explain why current revision differed at the two points in time. The original record, in turn, serves only to preserve the initial divergence and the action of stopping retries. With the two kept separate, readers can accept both "a page was usable later" and "the initial divergence remains unexplained" as facts.

If the same object shows two states again, the first step is to record separately whether the original request is attached, the time the page was displayed, whether collection is enabled, and whether execution is enabled. Without this material, screenshots can only serve as attachments documenting the incident, and cannot be used to fill in the request conditions. New observations should not overwrite the original record preserved this time either.

## What Remains Unconfirmed

There is currently no material showing under which request condition the two revision values began to differ, nor any material showing whether serializer hook was involved. It is also unconfirmed whether any original records can still be retrieved apart from the expired job. The recovery result for nested configuration can only be tied to the point in time represented by the recovery page, and cannot answer these three open questions.

The incident file remains `docs/adj-amqp/incidents/amqp-documentation-portal-two-states-for-one-object.md`. When reviewing it, read the original record, the recovery page, and the later card records separately. HCFE-006, HCFE-007, HCFE-013 provide reference points for the supplemental handoff record, the separate incident timeline, and the entry point collection state, respectively; they do not combine into a single root cause.

This postmortem preserves the sequence and wording from the old record that are no longer entirely accurate: the entry point divergence was observed first, then the records were saved and retries were stopped, and only afterward were partial recovery and the gap in the logs observed. It explains why the state at the time was not overwritten further, and which later assessments cannot be projected back any further; the relationship between the original request and serializer hook remains unconfirmed.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

The team's approach to maintaining the shared entry point needs to be settled first in this review round. The existing collections-and-consumers entry is still used to look up component relationships; at the same time, the component split has left an adjustment window. These two should not be treated as the same entry: the former is a lookup location known to readers, while the latter is only a scope of work for handling boundary adjustments.

Decision: retain the collections-and-consumers entry; do not designate the adjustment window as a replacement entry. Within the window, changes that have already been jointly checked can be handled, but the actual impact, coordinator, and old entry eligible for withdrawal should be recorded for each change. The old entry is not a cleanup target yet; until the new relationships have been jointly clarified, it retains value as a lookup reference.

The review does not begin by grouping according to implementation ownership. The repository directory tree, package list, and focused tests are materials to examine together. First write down the relationships that can be observed, then discuss who maintains the implementation; otherwise, directory locations, package boundaries, and test locations can easily be conflated as the same kind of rationale.

Those who support making the adjustment directly worry that the old entry will obscure the new component boundaries. Those who favor retaining the entry worry that users will first lose the known path. This review round did not deny the former concern; it simply did not treat it as grounds for immediately replacing the entry.

Focused tests were previously traced back through `src/reactive-x/tests/Cases/ObservableTest.php` and the related call names. This file is a verification point, not the permanent home of the shared entry point. The coordinator's specific arrangements will be added in a later handoff record.
