# Public Entry Point Maintenance Decision Record

As the component split progressed, collections-and-consumers remained a public location repeatedly mentioned by the team. Its original role was not to identify ownership of a particular implementation file, but to let readers continue tracing component relationships from a known location. After the split began, two different expectations emerged around it: some wanted to preserve this path so existing consumers would not lose their bearings during the adjustments; others wanted to use the adjustment window to consolidate the old organizational structure as soon as possible, giving the new component boundaries a more direct home.

The draft described this as "retain the entry point while making adjustments as the split proceeds". The review found that this sentence compressed two actions into one vague judgment. Retaining the entry point answers where readers should look up relationships now; the adjustment window answers the scope within which the team can reorganize existing boundaries. The existence of a window does not automatically make it a new public entry point. Nor is an ongoing split, by itself, a reason to remove the old entry point.

This decision retains the current collections-and-consumers entry point. The adjustment window can accommodate local changes supported by the existing materials, but it cannot replace the existing entry point, nor can it require consumers to understand the internal adjustments before they can find the original relationships. The decision is limited to entry point continuity and adjustment records; it does not assign final directories to all components in advance, nor does it treat any single reorganization as proof that the boundaries have stabilized.

The approaches compared during the review were not complicated, but they addressed different problems.

| Approach | What it was intended to address at the time | Treatment in this round |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retain the collections-and-consers entry point | Let existing readers and consumers continue tracing component relationships from a known location | Retain as the public entry point |
| Replace the existing entry point with the adjustment window | Use the split as an opportunity to change the public location to the new organizational structure | Not adopted as a replacement |

collections-and-consers in the table above is the spelling used in the early notes; collections-and-consumers is used below to refer to the current entry point. That note is retained because the discussion at the time did indeed mix up the "entry point name" and the "window name"; what needed to change after review was the conclusion, not the record that this confusion had occurred.

Choosing to retain the entry point does not mean the old structure has been accepted as the final structure. The old entry point's continued existence only means that, within the scope that can be verified in this round, it still serves as the public lookup location. A reader may trace a location in the directory tree from here, may need to continue checking declarations in package manifests, or may use focused tests to confirm that a particular relationship is still observable. Each of these artifacts describes facts at a different level; the entry point keeps them from becoming scattered clues that can only be connected from memory.

The concerns raised by those supporting direct replacement also remain on record. If the old entry point remains unchanged for a long time, the new component boundaries may be visible only in local implementations or local discussions, while later readers continue to understand the overall component relationships through the old name. This is a valid concern that still needs to be addressed, but it does not justify "remove the old entry point now". Whether the new location already serves the same lookup role, and whether consumers can reconstruct the relationships through it, cannot be answered by the progress of the split alone.

Those opposing replacement were concerned about discontinuities during the switch. What readers previously found through collections-and-consumers was not necessarily a unified implementation; sometimes it was directory relationships, sometimes package boundaries, and sometimes observation points preserved on the test side. If the entry point is removed first and each area is then left to explain its new location, this may appear to eliminate one old name in the short term, but in practice it leaves every consumer to figure out the lookup path again. This cost arises not because the old name itself is important, but because the shared lookup path does not yet have a clear replacement.

The review retained the following working requirement:

> Treat the repository tree, package manifests, and focused tests as the shared map; record an observable contract before debating implementation ownership.

The shared map here does not require the directory tree, package manifests, and focused tests to give the same kind of answer. The directory tree shows how artifacts are currently laid out; package manifests show how boundaries are declared; focused tests provide actual observation points for some relationships. Bringing the three together is intended to keep the discussion grounded in known materials, not to qualify any one of them, on its own, to replace the entry point.

The discussion order has therefore changed to recording the observable contract first, then discussing implementation ownership. At a minimum, the observable contract must let participants explain clearly: which public location readers use to find relationships; which directories, declarations, or tests allow those relationships to be verified; and what will take over the original lookup path if the old entry point is withdrawn. Ownership discussions are still necessary, but they should not preempt these questions by renaming the entry point. Otherwise, even after an implementation has been assigned to a new boundary, package manifests and focused tests may still be interpreted according to the old relationships.

The draft listed the three types of materials together as the "basis for verification", but did not explain the differences in their roles in the decision. The additions after review introduce no new types of materials; they only tighten the judgment criteria: the directory tree, package manifests, and focused tests jointly define the scope that can be approved; no individual conjecture, expectation, or verbal naming is sufficient to elevate the adjustment window into a public entry point.

Local changes that already have corresponding materials are eligible for approval within the adjustment window. "Local" here does not mean that a change must be small, but that the relationships it affects can be seen. If a directory location changes, it must be possible to see whether a lookup relationship between the old and new locations is still preserved; if a declaration in a package manifest is adjusted, it must be possible to explain whether the path by which readers understand the boundary has changed; if focused tests are used to support a judgment, it must be possible to identify which relationship they observe. Where materials are missing, the record should remain unconfirmed rather than describing an expected effect as a completed entry point migration.

Every approved adjustment must leave three kinds of information: actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that can be withdrawn. These are not a formalized table, but three questions that must be answerable before the old path is withdrawn.

The actual impact describes what changed in the entry point relationships. It should not simply say "component split completed" or "reorganization finished". If public lookup moves from one location to another, it should explain whether the old location can still lead readers to the new relationships; if only a local declaration changes, it should also make clear that this has not been mistaken for a global entry point switch. Impacts that have not been observed may be left blank or unconfirmed; the goals of the component split cannot substitute for them.

The coordinator is responsible for bringing questions spanning multiple artifacts back into the same adjustment. This role is not the same as the long-term owner of the implementation. Directories, package declarations, and consumers' lookup habits may span different maintenance boundaries; coordination provides a point of contact for a particular entry point change, not a way to rewrite ownership of all components. The existing materials name no specific candidates, so this decision does not fill in a list of individuals as coordinators; when a handoff occurs, the actual arrangement should be recorded alongside the corresponding change.

The old entry point that can be withdrawn, in turn, addresses the exit path. It does not require the old structure to exist indefinitely, nor is it an unchanging compatibility commitment. It requires that, before withdrawal, a usable old path be left in place, along with an explanation of when that path no longer needs to be retained. If an adjustment later proves unsuitable, participants need to know where to return to the original relationships that could be verified; without that answer, the supposed withdrawal can only rely on the memories of those involved at the time.

The three kinds of information are kept in the same place because they constrain the consequences of a change, coordination across artifacts, and exit conditions, respectively. If they are split across different discussions, later readers may see only that the entry point was adjusted, without being able to find the adjustment's impact, who was responsible for connecting the questions, or under what conditions the old entry point was removed. They do not have to be completed by the same person either: implementers can provide impact descriptions, coordinators can handle questions across boundaries, and those retaining the old entry point can confirm that the lookup location is still available.

The review also revisited `src/reactive-x/tests/Cases/ObservableTest.php` and the related call names. This location can help confirm that some observation points still exist on the focused tests side, but that does not make it the permanent home of the public entry point. The draft only mentioned that it had been "traced through here", which could lead readers to mistake a lookup location for the location to which the entry point belongs; this revision explicitly separates the two.

Test file locations may change, and decisions about the public entry point should not be tied to a single file. If tests move, the directory tree, package manifests, and focused tests must still be considered together: whether directory relationships can still be found, whether declarations still explain the boundaries, and whether tests still make the relevant relationships observable. Conversely, even if a test file temporarily remains in its original location, that alone cannot prove that the old entry point should be retained permanently.

focused tests are not a stand-in for a release gate in this decision either. They are included in the shared map to prevent entry point adjustments from becoming detached from observable relationships. When tests can cover a relationship, participants must still check whether directories and package manifests leave readers with a corresponding lookup path; when tests cannot explain a relationship, the adjustment window should not be used to record that relationship as already stable. Tests, directories, and declarations may each have gaps, and the decision approves only the scope that can be explained by the existing materials.

The diagram below preserves the judgment sequence used in this round. It is not a component dependency diagram, nor does it indicate a sequence of calls among these materials; the arrows indicate the verification paths that must first converge in entry point maintenance discussions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[collections-and-consumers Entry point] --> B[Repository tree]
    A --> C[Package manifests]
    A --> D[focused tests]
    B --> E[Observable contract]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F[Local changes within the adjustment window]
    F --> G[Old entry point that can be withdrawn]
```

Placing the adjustment window after the observable contract in the diagram expresses the limitation of this round's decision: first examine what the existing materials can confirm, then determine which local changes can be made. It does not depict the adjustment window as a replacement node for collections-and-consumers. If a new public location emerges in the future, it will still be necessary to first explain how it takes over the lookup relationships provided by the old entry point, then separately discuss whether to withdraw the old path.

The reason for not adopting the replacement approach is not that "the old entry point is always better". The replacement approach has the advantage of forcing the team to confront new component boundaries earlier, and it may also reduce the cost of maintaining two names over the long term. The problem is that the materials for this round show only that the existing entry point is still used for lookup, and that directories, package manifests, and focused tests should jointly constrain the discussion; they do not show that a new public location has stabilized, or that consumers no longer depend on the old entry point. Directly elevating the window would treat "reorganization is permitted" and "it can be relied on" as the same thing.

The retention approach also has costs. The longer the old entry point remains, the more likely it is that new boundaries will appear only in local implementations, while public lookup remains under the old name. This risk should not be obscured by the decision to retain the entry point. When a new public location emerges later, its proposer needs to explain its relationship to collections-and-consumers, which known paths it will take over, and under what conditions the old entry point can be withdrawn. That explanation cannot merely cite "the components are being split", nor can it reach a conclusion based only on a single directory or test location.

What remains unresolved is: after a new public location emerges, how closely must the directory tree, package manifests, and focused tests correspond to support withdrawing the old entry point. The existing materials require approval within the scope covered by existing evidence, but provide no threshold based on a fixed count or a uniform format. This decision does not invent a set of thresholds, to avoid turning reservations raised during review into rules already in effect.

Another issue that must be filled in for specific changes is who will serve as coordinator. This round establishes only that every adjustment must leave coordination information; it does not designate the same long-term person in charge for all future adjustments. When entry point maintenance spans different artifacts, coordination arrangements may differ by change; fixing them in advance as component ownership would once again confuse "who drives this switch" with "who owns a particular implementation".

DOC-52 hold the handoff materials following the entry point switch. This record preserves why the adjustment window does not directly replace the existing entry point, and what information each local adjustment should retain. Handoff records should carry forward the impacts and coordination arrangements of specific changes, without reopening the full debate between the two approaches; when the entry point strategy needs to be reconsidered, return here to review the retention decision and the conditions that remain unresolved.

After review, the draft's phrase "adjust the entry point according to progress on the split" is no longer valid. The currently actionable judgment is: retain collections-and-consumers as the public lookup entry point; handle adjustments only within the scope that the directory tree, package manifests, and focused tests can already explain together; before withdrawing the old entry point, record the actual impact, a coordinator, and an old entry point that can be withdrawn. Other judgments concerning the new public location and withdrawal thresholds remain pending confirmation.

# Public Entry Maintenance Migration Procedure

When a public entry is about to move from the old entry to a candidate path, first identify all known users of context-and-coroutines. The list must identify callers still using the old entry; if the caller population is not listed, do not move the migration request forward.

In this round, allow only one user that can roll itself back to try the candidate path, while keeping the old entry in place. During the handoff, record the `src/http-server/src/Request.php` used for the lookup, the current caller, the failure symptoms during the trial, and the next person taking over. If no abnormality is observed, record that too; do not leave it blank.

Do not bring the remaining users along during the trial. If a failure occurs, first restore this caller's original old entry, then stop subsequent actions; the other known users remain on the old entry. Decide the next batch only after the caller population is complete.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance: Switchover Procedure

Switchovers for the shared entry point are handled in batches by consumer. The old entry point still serves some known consumers of context-and-coroutines; only one consumer that can roll back independently gets to try the candidate path first. The handoff must make two things clear: which caller has changed, and which batch of callers has not yet changed.

The earliest records contained only "old entry point" and "candidate path." That was not enough for someone else to take over: the scope was not tied to callers, and there was no way to know what to restore after a failure. The handoff unit is no longer the shared entry point's name. Instead, one reversible caller change is treated as one migration unit.

## Records to Leave Before Starting

Start with the list of known consumers. This list is not a master inventory that replaces searching. It is used only to confirm which callers still use the old entry point for this switchover and to select one candidate consumer from them. Consumers that are not named do not migrate with the trial; they continue calling the old entry point.

Record `src/http-server/src/Request.php` as the lookup anchor. It records where the entry point and call names were looked up at the time; it does not establish that file as the shared entry point's permanent home. The path must be followed by the actual name of the current caller. Generic labels such as "caller side" or "related location" do not let the next owner determine the boundary of this change.

The candidate consumer must meet one narrow condition: if it fails, its original call to the old entry point can be restored independently. If this cannot be confirmed, do not include it in this batch. Restoration here does not mean deleting the candidate path or requiring other consumers to roll back at the same time. It restores only the call for the one caller that ran the trial.

```text
Old entry point
  ├─ Known consumer A: keep using the old entry point
  ├─ Known consumer B: keep using the old entry point
  └─ Candidate consumer: try the candidate path
                    ├─ No issues: retain as a reference for the next review
                    └─ Failure observed: return this consumer to the old entry point
```

## Handoff Artifacts

For each trial, record four items: the source path, the current caller, the failure symptoms, and the next owner. Keep all four in the same record so the path is not in one place and the consumer in another, leaving the next owner to piece the scope together again.

Under failure symptoms, record only observed results. The candidate path being unusable, call results differing from those of the old entry point, or no observed issues are all valid entries; do not add unverified causes in this field. If the field is blank, the next person cannot tell whether there was no observation last time or the trial was never run this time.

Keep the next owner's actions limited as well: confirm that the specified caller can still return to the old entry point, check the observations in this record, then decide whether the list contains a clearly defined next item. Without the current caller or a restoration action, the migration has not moved forward. It cannot be marked complete merely because it was "handed off."

## Post-Trial Branches

After the candidate consumer switches to the candidate path, do not delete the old entry point. Observe only this one consumer's call results; do not migrate the other known consumers along with it. This keeps the restoration scope aligned with the change scope if a failure occurs, and keeps callers still using the old entry point out of the assessment of the new path.

If failure symptoms appear, first restore that consumer's original call to the old entry point, record the symptoms, then stop scheduling the next batch. Other consumers on the old entry point do not need to take any action. Completing the restoration does not mean the candidate path has been rejected; it only means this consumer will no longer participate in the trial.

If no issues are observed, this one consumer Fang Ke can serve as a reference for the next review, but that does not mean the shared entry point switchover is complete. The next batch still needs its caller, observations, and restoration method written out again; blanks or conclusions from the previous batch cannot simply be carried over. The first draft treated "able to run a trial" as roughly equivalent to "ready to continue migrating." After review, these remain two distinct judgments: the former establishes only that independent restoration is possible; the latter also requires a clearly defined next item on the list.

Supplementary entry-point lookup notes are in DOC-53. This page covers only the switchover handoff: first confirm the known consumers and the old entry point, then choose one consumer that can roll back independently to try the candidate path. If the next batch has not been named, do not expand this change.

Start at the repository's public entry point, then use `helper` and `phpunit` to locate the area around `src/cache/tests/Cases/StringHelperTest.php`. The code-reading order at the time was:

1. First look at the helper-related tests and call names in `StringHelperTest.php` to confirm what the tests actually interact with.
2. Follow one of the direct callers outward. Don't treat a same-named file as another call edge. Use the focused PHPUnit transcript only to check whether this lookup landed at the same test entry point.
3. From this caller, keep looking for the first real consumer of "team public entry point maintenance"; stop where an answer is needed from another owner.

This old page described the test file as more of a "public entry point" than it is now; keep that statement as the assessment made at the time. Looking back later, `StringHelperTest.php` is better treated as a signpost: it helps newcomers find test behavior near the entry point, but cannot by itself establish the entry point's permanent location.
